walkthroughs.title: Your first real conversation with ChatGPT
walkthroughs.description: Most people use ChatGPT like a search engine — type a fragment, hope for magic. That's not how it works. It's a reasoning engine: it generates the most statistically plausible continuation of whatever you give it. Which means quality of input is almost entirely predictive of quality of output. This walkthrough shows you what that means in practice.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: ChatGPT has no instinct for what you actually need — it only has what you wrote. Specificity isn't optional; it's the whole job.

steps.title: Open a blank chat and understand what you're working with
steps.content: Go to chat.openai.com and open a new chat. Each conversation is a self-contained context window. ChatGPT has no memory of previous sessions by default — it doesn't know who you are, what subject you teach, or what you've already tried. It knows only what you type, right now, in this window. This is not a flaw to work around. It's a design decision that gives you complete control over context.
steps.tip: Turn on Memory under Settings → Personalisation if you want ChatGPT to retain facts about you across sessions. It's off by default. Even with memory on, it's still helpful to re-state critical context at the start of a session — don't assume it remembered correctly.

steps.title: Write a deliberately bad prompt — and study the failure
steps.content: Type this exactly as written and read the entire response before moving on.
steps.code: explain AI
steps.warning: This will produce a generic, context-free response — usually a Wikipedia-level overview aimed at no one in particular. This is not a malfunction. ChatGPT responded precisely to what you gave it: an open-ended instruction with no audience, no depth, no format requirement, and no purpose. Every vague word is a decision the model has to make on your behalf. The response you got reflects every one of those defaults. The failure is in the prompt, not the model.

steps.title: Rewrite it with four specific constraints — compare the results
steps.content: Now run this version and compare the two responses side by side. Read both fully before moving on.
steps.code: Explain how neural networks learn, for a Class 10 student who has never studied programming. Use one real-world analogy. Keep it under 150 words.
steps.tip: Four things changed: audience, topic scope, format requirement, length constraint. Each one eliminates degrees of freedom the model was filling with defaults. You don't need all four every time. Even one specific constraint improves results meaningfully. The skill to develop is knowing which constraint matters most for the task you're doing: audience for teaching material, length for summaries, format for structured outputs, scope for avoiding tangents.

steps.title: Continue the thread — and feel the compounding context
steps.content: ChatGPT maintains the full conversation in its context window. You don't re-explain yourself — you build on what came before.
steps.code: Now rewrite the same explanation using a cricket match as the analogy instead.
steps.tip: Think of a conversation as a shared working document, not a series of independent queries. The longer and more consistent the thread, the more useful the outputs become — because the model has more context to reason from. The flip side: context bleed is real. If you pivot sharply to an unrelated topic mid-conversation, older context can subtly distort new answers. Start a new chat for genuinely new topics.

steps.title: Push back on the response — iteration is the real workflow
steps.content: The first response is a draft. Treat it that way. If something is wrong, unclear, or not what you needed, say so directly.
steps.code: That analogy doesn't quite work — cricket involves teams, but a neural network learns individually. Can you try again with a single-player analogy instead? Something a student in India would find familiar.
steps.tip: ChatGPT responds well to direct, specific criticism. 'This isn't right' is less useful than 'this is wrong because X — try Y instead.' The more you tell it what failed and why, the more precisely it can correct. Most good outputs come from three to five exchanges, not the first attempt.

walkthroughs.title: Custom instructions: make GPT remember your context
walkthroughs.description: Every new chat starts from zero. ChatGPT doesn't know your name, your subject, your students' level, or what matters to you. Custom instructions fix this. You write once what's permanently true about you, and the model applies it silently to every response — without you having to repeat yourself every session.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Custom instructions are ambient context. They don't constrain GPT — they free you from re-explaining yourself 50 times a week.

steps.title: Find the settings
steps.content: Click your profile icon in the bottom-left corner → select 'Customise ChatGPT'. You'll see two text fields. What you write here persists across every new conversation. It's not part of the conversation history — it runs invisibly before every response.

steps.title: Fill out 'What should ChatGPT know about you?' with specific facts
steps.content: This field changes what 'accurate' means. It's not about preferences — it's about giving the model the facts it needs to stop making wrong assumptions about who it's talking to. Be specific about your context: subject, level, location, constraints, and anything that makes your situation different from the generic user.
steps.code: I'm a Class 9 science teacher at a CBSE school in Pune, India. My students speak English as a second language — most are more comfortable in Marathi or Hindi. Our school doesn't have a functional lab, so all demonstrations must be paper-based or use readily available household materials. I typically prepare materials 48 hours in advance and can't always revise at the last minute.
steps.tip: The more your context diverges from the default user the model imagines — typically a tech-literate adult in the US or UK — the more important this field becomes. Don't be modest about specifics. 'India' is more useful than 'South Asia'. 'CBSE Class 9' is more useful than 'secondary school'. 'No functional lab' is more useful than 'limited resources'.

steps.title: Fill out 'How should ChatGPT respond?' with format preferences
steps.content: This is the how, not the who. Specify tone, format norms, things you always want, and things you never want. Focus on the 20% of preferences that affect 80% of your interactions — don't try to anticipate every edge case.
steps.code: Keep explanations concise: one clear idea per paragraph. When generating exam questions, always label each question with its Bloom's taxonomy level in brackets (e.g. [Recall], [Application]). When you're uncertain about a fact, say so explicitly — don't present uncertainty with false confidence. Default to metric units and use Indian curriculum contexts and examples. Don't add a 'hope this helps' or similar closing.
steps.tip: These are defaults, not mandates. You can always override in the conversation itself — 'write a very detailed explanation' will override a 'keep it concise' instruction. The conversation always takes priority over the background instructions.

steps.title: Test it — immediately and honestly
steps.content: Open a new chat and ask something simple and work-related. Compare the output tone, format, and examples to what you'd have gotten before. Look specifically for: Did it default to Indian curriculum examples? Did it avoid filler phrases? Is the length appropriate?
steps.code: Give me three engaging hooks I can use to open a lesson on friction for Class 9 students.
steps.warning: Custom instructions don't override explicit in-conversation instructions. If you ask for a very long detailed explanation in a chat, you'll get one — even if your instructions say to keep things concise. Also worth knowing: custom instructions are not encrypted. Anthropic can see them. Don't put anything sensitive in there.

walkthroughs.title: Using ChatGPT for lesson planning
walkthroughs.description: ChatGPT is an excellent first-draft engine for lesson materials — fast, flexible, and capable of generating differentiated content on demand. The risk is treating those drafts as finished products. This walkthrough covers an honest workflow: what to generate, what to verify, and where teacher judgment is non-negotiable.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: ChatGPT saves time on generation. It doesn't replace judgment on pedagogy, cultural fit, syllabus accuracy, or your specific class.

steps.title: Start with a fully-specified prompt — not just a topic
steps.content: The most common mistake: giving ChatGPT only a topic and expecting a usable lesson plan. You'll get something generic and unfocused. Specify the standard or chapter, the grade, the board, the time, what students already know, and what the lesson needs to achieve.
steps.code:
Create a 45-minute lesson plan for Class 8 CBSE students on 'Friction' from the Science curriculum. Prior knowledge: students understand forces and motion. Include:
- A 5-minute hook that doesn't require equipment
- 15 minutes of concept explanation with at least one analogy
- 15 minutes of activity using standard classroom materials only
- 10 minutes of formative assessment (not a written quiz)
Format: clear sections with both teacher instructions and expected student responses.
steps.tip: Name your board (CBSE/ICSE/State), the exact chapter or standard, the class level, and any specific constraints like 'no internet access' or 'multi-level class'. Each constraint narrows the model's degrees of freedom and produces more targeted output.

steps.title: Generate differentiated versions without starting over
steps.content: Once you have a working base plan, ask ChatGPT to produce three versions of the concept explanation for different learner levels. This is one of the highest-ROI uses of the tool — what would take 90 minutes manually takes 2 minutes.
steps.code:
Based on this lesson plan, create three versions of the 'friction' concept explanation:
1. For students who are struggling: very simple language, more analogies, no technical vocabulary in the first read
2. For on-grade students: standard explanation as in the original plan
3. For advanced students: include real engineering applications — why friction matters in brake design, road engineering, or shoe manufacturing
steps.tip: Ask for one level at a time if the output feels rushed. ChatGPT tends to rush when generating three versions simultaneously — you get shorter, less carefully differentiated content. Two separate requests often produce better results than one combined request.

steps.title: Generate assessment questions at specific cognitive levels
steps.content: Rather than asking for 'some questions', specify the cognitive distribution using Bloom's taxonomy. This gives you assessment that's actually differentiated in difficulty and thinking demand.
steps.code:
Create 8 assessment questions on friction for Class 8 CBSE, distributed as follows:
- 2 recall questions (definition-level, no application required)
- 3 application questions (use friction to explain a real-world situation)
- 2 analysis questions (compare types of friction, explain why friction varies by surface)
- 1 evaluation question (student must take a position and justify it)
For each question, include the expected answer and the Bloom's level in brackets.
steps.warning: Always check that examples are culturally appropriate for your students. ChatGPT frequently defaults to Western contexts — car brakes on ice, ice skating rinks, American football cleats. Swap these for locally relevant examples: auto-rickshaw brakes, monsoon roads, rubber chappals on a wet floor. The concepts are identical; the examples matter for student engagement and comprehension.

steps.title: Know exactly what ChatGPT cannot do in this workflow
steps.content:
ChatGPT is a generation tool, not a pedagogy expert for your specific context. There are four things it consistently cannot do well:

1. Verify whether content matches your exact board syllabus — always cross-check against the official curriculum document.
2. Know what your specific class already understands — it models an average student, not your students.
3. Catch culturally inappropriate content — a festival analogy that's irrelevant to your region, a sport your students don't play.
4. Replace your professional assessment of pacing — a plan that looks right on paper may be too fast or too slow for your class.
steps.warning: Read everything before sharing with students. Factual errors appear in AI-generated lesson content — especially in science, where examples sometimes reflect outdated knowledge. You are responsible for everything that reaches your classroom. 'The AI wrote it' is not a defence.

walkthroughs.title: What ChatGPT gets wrong — and how to catch it
walkthroughs.description: ChatGPT is confidently wrong more often than most users realise. It doesn't know when it doesn't know something — it generates what sounds right. Understanding the specific categories of failure makes you much better at catching errors before they matter.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: The most dangerous ChatGPT outputs are the ones that are almost right. Obvious nonsense is easy to catch. Plausible-sounding errors with wrong details slip through.

steps.title: Hallucination: plausible facts that didn't happen
steps.content: ChatGPT will invent citations, statistics, dates, names, and events that sound entirely plausible. It doesn't lie — it generates the most statistically likely continuation of your prompt. If your prompt points toward a specific type of answer, it will generate that type of answer whether or not the facts exist.
steps.code:
Test this yourself:
Ask: 'What research studies support spaced repetition as a learning technique? Give me three specific citations with authors and journal names.'

Then: Search for those citations on Google Scholar. Count how many actually exist.
steps.warning: Expect at least one to be fabricated or significantly wrong. The title might be real, the journal might be real, but the year, the authors, and the actual findings are frequently confabulated. Never cite an AI-provided reference without independently verifying it exists.

steps.title: Currency: it doesn't know what happened recently
steps.content: ChatGPT's knowledge has a training cutoff. It doesn't know about events, policies, curriculum changes, or research published after that date. For stable topics (photosynthesis, the French Revolution, basic grammar), this doesn't matter. For anything that changes — board exam patterns, government schemes, recent research — it may be out of date without telling you.
steps.tip: For anything where recency matters, use Perplexity or Google instead. ChatGPT is good at reasoning from stable knowledge, not at tracking what changed recently.

steps.title: Specificity collapse: it generalises when you need local accuracy
steps.content: Ask ChatGPT about the CBSE Class 10 Science syllabus and it will produce something that looks correct but may include chapters that don't exist, omit actual chapters, or describe content from a different year's syllabus. It doesn't have reliable access to specific institutional documents — it generalises from patterns in its training data.
steps.code:
Test:
'What chapters are covered in CBSE Class 10 Science?'

Then open the actual NCERT textbook or the CBSE curriculum document and compare. Note any differences.
steps.warning: Syllabus details, exam patterns, government scheme specifics, and institutional policies should always be verified against primary sources. ChatGPT is useful for explaining concepts within a syllabus — not for accurately describing the syllabus itself.

steps.title: How to build a verification reflex
steps.content:
You don't need to verify everything ChatGPT produces — that would defeat the purpose. You need to verify the things that matter:

- Any specific statistic (verify: where did this number come from?)
- Any citation (verify: does it exist, does it say this?)
- Anything about your specific board, syllabus, or exam (verify: check the primary document)
- Anything that will be shared with students as fact

Everything else — generated drafts, explanations of concepts you already understand, structural suggestions — can be used with normal professional judgment.
steps.tip: Build one habit: before you share any AI-generated factual claim with students, ask yourself 'can I verify this in 60 seconds?' If yes, spend the 60 seconds. If you can't verify it quickly, either verify it properly or don't share it.

walkthroughs.title: What makes Claude different from ChatGPT
walkthroughs.description: Claude and ChatGPT are not interchangeable. They make different tradeoffs, have different strengths, and behave differently in ways that matter for practical use. This guide is not about which is better — it's about when to use which one.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Use Claude when you need depth, nuance, and honesty about uncertainty. Use ChatGPT when you need speed, breadth, and ecosystem integrations.

steps.title: The core difference: how they handle uncertainty
steps.content:
The most practically significant difference between Claude and ChatGPT is not intelligence — it's epistemic honesty. Claude is significantly more likely to say 'I'm not sure about this' or 'you should verify this claim'. ChatGPT more often presents uncertain information with confident tone.

This isn't because Claude is less capable. It's a deliberate design difference. For educational use, it changes how you should read outputs: ChatGPT output requires more active verification; Claude output tends to flag where verification is needed.
steps.tip: Neither approach is universally better. Confident incorrect output is dangerous in academic contexts. But excessive hedging ('I might be wrong about this but possibly...') makes some tasks slower and more frustrating. Know which you're getting.

steps.title: Where Claude is clearly stronger: long documents and complex reasoning
steps.content:
Claude has a very large context window and handles long, dense material well. It can reason across an entire academic paper, hold contradictions across sections in mind simultaneously, and produce structured analysis of long-form material without drifting.

For tasks like: 'read this 40-page curriculum document and identify all places where concept A is expected to have been taught before topic B is introduced' — Claude is the right choice.
steps.code:
Things Claude is better at than ChatGPT:
- Analysing long documents (textbooks, papers, policy documents)
- Maintaining argument coherence across a long response
- Nuanced writing that sounds like a human, not an AI template
- Acknowledging what it doesn't know
- Handling ambiguous, open-ended questions without forcing a tidy answer

steps.title: Where ChatGPT is clearly stronger: ecosystem and breadth
steps.content: ChatGPT has a larger plugin and integration ecosystem. It has DALL-E image generation built in. It has a larger library of custom GPTs for specific tasks. It tends to be faster for quick tasks. For multimodal tasks (image generation + text together), for accessing the GPT Store's specialised tools, or for tasks requiring internet access — ChatGPT is the better choice.
steps.code:
Things ChatGPT is better at than Claude:
- Image generation (via DALL-E, built in)
- Integrations with third-party tools via the GPT Store
- Quick, surface-level tasks where speed matters
- Code generation and execution (Code Interpreter)
- Broader general knowledge for topics not requiring deep analysis

steps.title: The practical rule: use both, task by task
steps.content: The question is never 'which AI should I use' — it's 'which tool matches this specific task'. Once you've used both for a few weeks, you'll develop an instinct for this. Until then, use the shorthand below.
steps.code:
Use Claude when:
- You're working with a long or complex document
- You need nuanced, argument-rich writing
- Accuracy matters more than speed
- You want to be told when something is uncertain

Use ChatGPT when:
- You need something fast and 'good enough'
- You need image generation
- You're using a third-party integration
- You want a quick draft to iterate on

walkthroughs.title: Uploading and analysing documents with Claude
walkthroughs.description: Most AI tools treat documents as context to summarise. Claude treats them as material to reason about. The difference shows up when you ask hard questions — not 'what does this say' but 'what's missing', 'what's contradictory', 'what would a careful critic challenge'. This walkthrough covers the questions worth asking.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Don't ask Claude to summarise. Ask it to interrogate. You can already read — the value is in what a second analytical pass reveals.

steps.title: Upload the document
steps.content: Click the paperclip icon or drag the file into the chat. Claude handles PDFs, Word documents, plain text, and more. For classroom use: a textbook chapter, research paper, curriculum document, syllabus, student essay, or mark scheme all work. Claude's context window is large — a full academic paper or a 100-page chapter fits without chunking or summarising first.
steps.tip: Upload multiple documents at once for cross-document analysis. 'What does each of these three sources say about X?' or 'Where do these documents contradict each other?' are questions that take full advantage of Claude's ability to hold multiple texts in context simultaneously.

steps.title: Ask questions that require judgment, not just reading
steps.content: The worst use of Claude on a document is asking it to 'summarise this' — you get a shorter, flatter version of something you already have. Instead, ask questions that require analytical work: interpretation, identification of gaps, structural analysis, argument critique.
steps.code:
Questions worth asking about any document:

'What are the three claims in this text that are least supported by the evidence provided?'

'What does the author assume the reader already believes before they start reading?'

'If a well-informed critic wanted to challenge this argument, what's the weakest point they'd attack?'

'What important questions does this document leave unanswered?'

'What is the author not saying — what's notably absent from this account?'
steps.tip: These questions work on textbook chapters, research papers, policy documents, student essays, and school handbooks — any document with structure or argument. The more specific your question, the more specific and useful Claude's analysis will be.

steps.title: Generate curriculum materials grounded in the actual text
steps.content: Materials generated from an uploaded document are anchored to that specific text — not to Claude's general training knowledge. This is the key advantage: no drift into off-syllabus examples, no generic content that doesn't match your chapter.
steps.code:
Based on this chapter, generate:
1. Five exam questions: two recall, two application, one evaluation. Include the expected answer for each and the specific section of the chapter the answer comes from.
2. The eight most important vocabulary terms with student-facing definitions that a Class 9 student could understand.
3. A 200-word plain-English summary suitable for student revision.
4. Three common misconceptions about this topic that students often hold, and a one-sentence correction for each.
steps.tip: Ask Claude to quote the relevant section of the document when answering a factual question. This gives you a direct reference, speeds up verification, and prevents Claude from filling gaps with general knowledge.

steps.title: Use it to give structured feedback on student writing
steps.content: Upload a student essay or answer. Provide the assignment prompt and a rubric — or ask Claude to generate a rubric from the prompt first. Then ask for structured, levelled feedback.
steps.code:
Assignment prompt: [paste your prompt here]

Student response: [paste the student's work]

Evaluate this response against three criteria:
1. Accuracy and completeness of content
2. Clarity of argument and logical structure
3. Quality and specificity of evidence used

For each criterion: a score out of 5, one specific strength with a direct quote from the student's work, and one specific area to improve with a concrete suggestion. Keep the tone appropriate for a Class 10 student receiving written feedback.
steps.warning: Claude is a useful first-pass feedback tool, but it doesn't know your student. It can't distinguish between a student who hasn't engaged with the material and one who is struggling with written English. Always read the generated feedback before sharing it. Adjust the tone and specificity for students who might find direct feedback discouraging.

steps.title: Cross-document analysis: where it becomes genuinely powerful
steps.content: Upload two or more documents simultaneously and ask comparative questions. This is difficult to do manually and is one of the most underused capabilities of the tool.
steps.code:
Upload: your school's official science curriculum + an NCERT textbook chapter

Ask: 'Does the textbook chapter cover all the learning objectives in the curriculum document? If not, what's missing or underemphasised?'

Or upload: two research papers on the same topic

Ask: 'Where do these two papers agree, where do they disagree, and what does each say that the other doesn't address?'
steps.tip: Name the documents clearly in your prompt ('in Document 1...' or 'in the curriculum document vs the textbook chapter...') to help Claude keep them distinct in its analysis.

walkthroughs.title: Projects: give Claude persistent context across sessions
walkthroughs.description: Every new Claude conversation normally starts from scratch. Projects change that. You create a persistent workspace where you upload documents, set instructions, and build context that carries across every conversation in that project. For ongoing work — a unit you're teaching, a research topic you're developing, a school policy you're working on — Projects are the feature that makes Claude genuinely useful over time rather than just for one-off tasks.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Projects are persistent context. Everything you add — documents, instructions, conversation history — accumulates and informs every new conversation within that project.

steps.title: Create a project and set its context
steps.content: On the Claude.ai sidebar, click 'New Project'. Give it a descriptive name. Then: write a project system prompt in the instructions field. This is the persistent background context that runs before every conversation in this project. It should describe who you are, what the project is about, what you need, and any constraints.
steps.code:
Example project instruction for a Class 9 Chemistry unit:

'I am a Class 9 Chemistry teacher (CBSE) preparing materials for the unit on Atoms and Molecules. My students speak English as a second language and respond better to analogies and visual descriptions than to abstract definitions. I am uploading: the NCERT chapter, my school's curriculum scope, and last year's exam paper. All materials I generate should be appropriate for this level, should follow CBSE curriculum standards, and should use Indian-context examples where possible.'

steps.title: Upload your documents once — reference them indefinitely
steps.content: Inside the project, upload your source documents. They stay there permanently — you don't re-upload every time. Every conversation in this project can reference them directly without you having to paste content or re-explain what you're working on.
steps.tip: Upload the documents that represent your 'ground truth' for this project: the official syllabus, the textbook chapters, the exam mark schemes. These become the authoritative reference Claude draws from in every conversation.

steps.title: Use conversation history as accumulated knowledge
steps.content: Within a project, conversations accumulate. Previous exchanges become visible context. If you developed a particular lesson plan format in an earlier conversation, you can reference it: 'Use the same format as the friction lesson we developed last week.' Claude can access the conversation history within the project.
steps.tip: Keep project conversations focused by topic. One conversation for lesson planning, another for assessment design, another for student feedback templates. This keeps the context clean and prevents one thread contaminating another.

steps.title: Build domain-specific intelligence over time
steps.content: The longer you work in a project, the more context Claude has about your specific situation. After several weeks of work on a unit, it will have encountered your students' specific difficulties, your preferred formats, the constraints of your school, and the decisions you've made about how to teach particular concepts.
steps.code:
Practical projects worth creating:

- 'Class 9 Science Unit: Atoms and Molecules' — all materials for one unit
- 'Student Assessment Bank' — exam questions, mark schemes, feedback templates
- 'Lesson Plan Templates' — your developed formats and examples
- 'Research Project: [topic]' — for personal or professional development research
- 'School Policy Documentation' — if you're doing admin or curriculum work
steps.warning: Claude's memory within a project has limits. Very long conversation threads may start losing context from earlier exchanges. For highly important decisions or formats developed in a project, save them explicitly in a document you upload back to the project — don't rely on conversation history alone.

walkthroughs.title: Using Perplexity for research you can actually verify
walkthroughs.description: Every AI tool will give you an answer. Perplexity is the only one that shows you where the answer came from, in a form you can actually check. This changes the nature of the task: you're not just reading the answer, you're using it to find the sources. The citation is the output; the text is just the map.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: If you're not clicking through to at least one source every research session, you're using Perplexity wrong. The citation is the point.

steps.title: Ask synthesis questions, not lookup questions
steps.content: Perplexity earns its keep on questions that require pulling together multiple sources — not single-answer lookups you could Google in 15 seconds. 'What year was X born' is a Google question. 'What does recent research say about X and what are its limitations' is a Perplexity question.
steps.code:
High-value Perplexity question patterns:

'What does current research say about [topic]? What are the most important limitations of the evidence?'

'What are the main disagreements among researchers on [topic]? Who holds which positions?'

'What happened with [policy/event] over the last 12 months? Summarise the key developments.'

'What are the strongest arguments for and against [position]? With sources for each.'
steps.tip: Add 'what are the limitations of this evidence' or 'are there contradictory studies' to almost any research question. Perplexity will surface the caveats if you ask for them — but it won't volunteer them if you don't.

steps.title: Click through to every source you plan to use — without exception
steps.content: After getting a response, identify the most important claim — the one you'd use in your work or share with students. Find the numbered citation next to it. Click it. Go to the actual source. Read the abstract or the relevant section. Ask yourself: does the source actually say what Perplexity claimed?
steps.warning: Perplexity misrepresents sources. Not constantly, but frequently enough that you can't skip this step. The mismatch is usually subtle: the source does exist and does address the topic, but the specific claim Perplexity attributed to it is slightly wrong — a different finding, a different direction, a finding that's hedged in the original but stated as fact in the summary. The citation tells you where to find the truth. It doesn't mean Perplexity found it correctly.

steps.title: Build a chain of follow-up questions
steps.content: The best Perplexity session isn't one question — it's a directed chain that moves from broad to specific. Each follow-up inherits the context of the previous exchange.
steps.code:
Example chain for education research:

1. 'What does research say about the effectiveness of formative assessment in secondary schools?'

2. 'Which of these studies had the largest sample sizes and longest follow-up periods?'

3. 'Are there studies specifically on formative assessment in Indian secondary schools, or in other low-to-middle income country contexts?'

4. 'What does this research say about implementation challenges — what makes formative assessment difficult to sustain in practice?'
steps.tip: You can reference a specific source from a previous response: 'The third source in your last answer — what else does that research group say about this topic?' Perplexity can often go deeper into a specific source or author.

steps.title: Use Focus mode to narrow the source pool
steps.content: Perplexity's Focus settings let you restrict results to: web (default), academic papers, YouTube, Reddit, or specific sources. For serious research, switching to Academic focuses the output on peer-reviewed papers and preprints — much higher signal-to-noise than general web results.
steps.tip: Academic mode is slower but substantially more reliable for claims about research evidence. Use it any time you need to cite something or share a finding with students as established research.

walkthroughs.title: Pro Search mode: deep research on any topic
walkthroughs.description: Standard Perplexity gives you a synthesis with citations. Pro Search goes further: it reasons about what sub-questions need to be answered to address your query, searches for each one separately, and synthesises a more complete answer. For complex research questions, the difference in output quality is significant.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Pro Search isn't just a better search — it's a multi-step research process that anticipates the sub-questions your main question implies.

steps.title: Understand what Pro Search actually does differently
steps.content: In standard search, Perplexity takes your query, searches for relevant results, and synthesises them. In Pro Search, it first breaks your query into sub-questions, searches for each one, then synthesises across all the results. You can see the intermediate questions it generated — this gives you insight into how it's decomposing your problem.
steps.tip: The intermediate questions Perplexity generates in Pro Search are often useful in themselves. They show you what dimensions of your research question exist and give you a ready-made list of follow-up queries.

steps.title: Use it for genuinely complex research questions
steps.content: Pro Search is overkill for simple queries. It adds time and complexity. Use it for questions that require evidence from multiple distinct angles — where a single-search synthesis would miss important nuance.
steps.code:
Good Pro Search questions:

'What are the educational outcomes of one-to-one device programmes in developing country secondary schools? Include both positive findings and null or negative findings.'

'How has the consensus on [contested topic in your subject] changed over the last 10 years, and what drove those changes?'

'What are the main implementation challenges reported by teachers using AI tools in classrooms, across different country contexts?'

steps.title: Evaluate the sub-questions it generated
steps.content: When Pro Search shows you its intermediate steps, read the sub-questions it chose to research. Ask yourself: are these the right sub-questions? Are there important ones it missed? If so, run those as explicit follow-up queries.
steps.code:
After Pro Search completes:

1. Read the sub-questions it generated
2. Identify any important sub-question it didn't ask
3. Run that as a follow-up: 'You didn't address [angle]. What does the evidence say about this specifically?'
steps.warning: Pro Search can produce impressive-looking comprehensive answers that still contain specific factual errors. The volume and structure of the output can create a false sense of authority. Citation verification is more important, not less, with Pro Search.

walkthroughs.title: Upload your syllabus and ask questions about it
walkthroughs.description: NotebookLM is different from every other AI tool on this list in one fundamental way: it cannot use anything outside your uploaded sources. It won't supplement from its own knowledge, it won't fill gaps with plausible-sounding content, and it won't answer questions your documents don't answer — it tells you it can't. That constraint is the feature.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: NotebookLM is the right tool when accuracy to a specific source matters more than breadth. It's the only AI tool that literally cannot wander off into its own knowledge.

steps.title: Create a focused notebook and upload your source documents
steps.content: Go to notebooklm.google.com. Click 'New Notebook'. Give it a specific name ('Class 9 Science — Atoms and Molecules unit', not 'Science stuff'). Upload your source documents: PDFs, Google Docs, pasted text, or URLs. For a single unit, upload: the textbook chapter, the official curriculum/syllabus page, any supplementary readings you've assigned, and last year's exam paper if you have it.
steps.tip: Create separate notebooks per unit or subject — not one massive notebook for everything. The more focused the source set, the more accurate and specific the answers. A notebook with 5 highly relevant documents produces better output than one with 30 loosely related ones.

steps.title: Ask questions only your sources can answer
steps.content: The highest-value questions are the ones where you want the answer to come from your specific documents, not from general knowledge. Syllabus compliance, curriculum-specific vocabulary, exam-specific requirements — these are questions where hallucination from general knowledge is dangerous.
steps.code:
Questions worth asking:

'According to the official curriculum document, what are the stated learning objectives for this unit?'

'Which vocabulary terms does the textbook explicitly define in this chapter?'

'What practical activities does the curriculum document recommend for teaching this concept?'

'Based on the exam papers I uploaded, what types of questions appear most frequently for this topic?'

'Do the textbook and the curriculum document agree on how to define [term]? Quote both.'
steps.warning: NotebookLM will tell you if a question can't be answered from your sources. This is correct behaviour — it's not a failure. If you keep hitting this wall, either your question is outside the scope of what you uploaded, or you need to add more source documents.

steps.title: Generate curriculum-anchored study materials
steps.content: Because everything is grounded in your uploads, generated materials are accurate to your specific documents — not to a generic version of the topic.
steps.code:
Ask for:

'Create a revision guide from these sources with: (1) all key terms the textbook defines, with the exact definition from the text, (2) the main concepts in the sequence they appear in the chapter, (3) 8 questions that could appear on the exam based on the past papers I uploaded, with expected answers grounded in the textbook.'

Or: 'Based on the curriculum document and the textbook, identify any place where what the curriculum requires and what the textbook explains don't fully align.'

steps.title: Use the Audio Overview for revision
steps.content: Click 'Audio Overview' in the right panel. NotebookLM generates a 10–15 minute podcast-style dialogue between two voices discussing the key ideas in your uploaded material. It synthesises and connects ideas rather than just reading text back. Useful for revision while commuting, or in class as a warm-up activity for students who have been assigned reading.
steps.tip: The Audio Overview is generated from your specific sources, so it reflects your actual uploaded content. Two notebooks on the same topic but with different source documents will produce different audio overviews. This makes it genuinely curriculum-specific, not generic revision content.

walkthroughs.title: Using NotebookLM to compare sources and find contradictions
walkthroughs.description: One of the most underused features of NotebookLM is cross-document analysis. When you have multiple sources that address the same topic — multiple textbooks, multiple papers, multiple policy documents — NotebookLM can identify where they agree, where they disagree, and what each says that the others don't.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: NotebookLM with multiple sources is the most efficient tool for identifying contradictions and gaps across a document set — because every answer is cited and traceable.

steps.title: Upload multiple sources on the same topic
steps.content: For comparison analysis, upload at least two sources that address the same topic: two textbooks, two research papers, an official curriculum document and a textbook, a policy statement and an implementation guide. Label them in your prompt by name so NotebookLM keeps them distinct.
steps.tip: For academic or professional use: upload your primary source and two or three secondary sources that discuss it. NotebookLM can then help you identify which secondary sources engage most closely with the primary, and where they misread or selectively quote it.

steps.title: Ask explicit comparison questions with citation requirements
steps.content: Ask questions that force NotebookLM to draw from multiple sources and show its work. Always ask for citations so you can verify the comparison.
steps.code:
'How does Source A define [term] compared to Source B? Quote both definitions.'

'Where do these two sources disagree about [concept]? Quote the specific passages that contradict each other.'

'What does Source A say about [topic] that Source B doesn't address at all?'

'If I had to reconcile these two accounts, where would the main tension be?'

steps.title: Use contradiction-finding for curriculum alignment
steps.content: A practical classroom application: upload your school's curriculum document alongside the textbook chapters. Ask NotebookLM to identify where the textbook's coverage doesn't fully satisfy the curriculum's stated requirements. This surfaces gaps you might otherwise only discover when grading a student's exam response.
steps.code: 'Compare what the curriculum document says students should be able to do by the end of this unit with what the textbook chapter actually teaches. Identify any learning objective in the curriculum that is not clearly addressed in the textbook.'
steps.warning: NotebookLM's cross-document analysis is only as good as your uploads. If the curriculum document is vague or the textbook is poorly structured, the comparison will reflect those limitations. You may need to do a manual check on anything it says is 'not covered' — it may be covered but in language too different for NotebookLM to match.

walkthroughs.title: Your first image: understanding the prompt anatomy
walkthroughs.description: Midjourney doesn't interpret vague intentions — it builds from concrete descriptions. The gap between 'make something cool' and getting exactly what you imagined is almost entirely about how you structure what you ask for. This walkthrough teaches the anatomy of a prompt that gives you control.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: An image prompt is not a caption — it's a specification. Subject, medium, style, lighting, composition, and mood are all separate levers. The more you specify, the more control you have.

steps.title: Set up access
steps.content: Midjourney runs inside Discord. Go to midjourney.com → Sign In → Join the Beta. Once in a server, find any newbies channel or invite the Midjourney bot to your own server. Type /imagine to open the prompt field. Midjourney also has a web interface at midjourney.com that some users find easier to navigate — same prompt logic applies.
steps.tip: If you're using Midjourney for educational content generation, create a private server and invite only the bot. This keeps your prompts and outputs in one organised place rather than scattered across public channels.

steps.title: Learn the five layers of a strong prompt
steps.content: A strong Midjourney prompt has five possible layers. You don't need all five every time — but understanding each layer tells you which lever to pull when you're not getting what you need.
steps.code:
The five layers:
[Subject] — what is the image about? Who or what is in it?
[Medium/Style] — is it a photograph, illustration, diagram, painting, sketch?
[Lighting] — studio, natural, dramatic, flat
[Composition] — close-up, wide angle, cross-section, overhead
[Mood/Atmosphere] — clinical, warm, neutral, dramatic

Full example:
'A human cell undergoing mitosis, scientific illustration, clean white background, cross-section view, textbook style, clearly labelled organelles'

Minimum viable example:
'A diagram of the water cycle, educational illustration style, clean and labelled'
steps.tip: 'Scientific illustration' and 'textbook style' are among the most useful style descriptors for educational use. They consistently pull outputs toward clear, diagrammatic, accurate-looking imagery rather than artistic or decorative interpretation.

steps.title: Run your first prompt and use the iteration controls
steps.content: Type /imagine and paste your prompt. Midjourney generates four image variants. Below each set you'll see U1–U4 (upscale a specific image to high resolution) and V1–V4 (generate four new variations based on that image). The reroll button generates four entirely new variants.
steps.code:
First prompt to try:
'A cross-section diagram of a plant cell, scientific illustration style, clean white background, all major organelles visible and labelled, textbook quality'

If you like image 2 but want variations: click V2
If image 1 is right: click U1 to get a high-resolution version
If none are right: click the reroll button for four new options
steps.tip: Don't start from scratch when you get something close but not right. V (variation) is almost always the faster path to your intended image than rewriting the prompt. Most good images come from three to five iteration steps, not the first attempt.

steps.title: Use it for educational content with appropriate care
steps.content: Midjourney is particularly effective for illustration-style educational content: diagrams, historical scene reconstructions, concept visualisations, and supporting imagery for presentations. The generated images are original and generally free from copyright concerns.
steps.code:
High-value patterns for educators:

'Diagram of [scientific concept], flat illustration, labelled, white background, educational style'

'Historical scene: [event description], illustration style, appropriate for secondary school'

'Infographic-style visual showing [process], clean layout, numbered steps'

'Portrait of [historical figure], editorial illustration, neutral background, no text' (for presentation slides)

'Map showing [geographical concept], simplified diagram, educational clarity over detail'
steps.warning: Midjourney generates plausible-looking but potentially wrong diagrams — anatomical structures with incorrect proportions, geographical maps with distorted or fabricated features, historical scenes with anachronistic details. Always review accuracy before classroom use, especially for scientific diagrams where visual accuracy matters.

steps.title: Understand what you cannot generate
steps.content: Midjourney's terms of service prohibit certain content, and its moderation filters block others. Understanding the limits saves you from wasted attempts.
steps.code:
You cannot generate:
- Realistic images of real, named, living people (politicians, celebrities, etc.)
- Explicit or violent content
- Content designed to deceive (fake news imagery, fabricated events)
- Trademarked characters (Disney, Marvel, etc.)

For educators specifically:
- Historical atrocities: Midjourney will generate stylised/illustrative representations but not graphic or photorealistic scenes
- Medical diagrams: it can generate these but accuracy is not guaranteed — always verify
steps.tip: For historical figures who are not living (Abraham Lincoln, Mahatma Gandhi), Midjourney can generate illustration-style portraits. Use the style descriptor 'editorial illustration' or 'historical portrait painting style' to ensure the output is clearly non-photographic.

walkthroughs.title: Generating educational diagrams and illustrations
walkthroughs.description: Midjourney is more capable of producing usable educational visuals than most educators realise — but it requires specific prompt patterns. Generic prompts produce generic results. This walkthrough covers the prompt formulas that consistently produce clean, classroom-appropriate diagrams and illustrations.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Educational diagrams need three things from Midjourney: a clear subject, an explicit style anchor, and constraints on clutter. Get those right and most science and social studies concepts are generatable in under 5 minutes.

steps.title: Use style anchors to control output type
steps.content: The single most important element for educational diagrams is the style anchor — a phrase that tells Midjourney what category of image you're targeting. Without a style anchor, you get an artistic interpretation. With a precise one, you get the diagram you need.
steps.code:
Style anchors and when to use each:

'scientific illustration style' — biology, chemistry, physics diagrams
'textbook diagram' — any concept requiring clean, labelled explanation
'educational infographic' — processes, timelines, comparisons
'flat vector diagram' — concept maps, flowcharts, system diagrams
'anatomical illustration style' — body systems, cell structure
'cross-section diagram' — anything requiring interior view
'historical illustration style' — history content, period-appropriate scenes
'topographic map style' or 'simplified political map' — geography

steps.title: Use negative prompts to remove clutter
steps.content: Midjourney often adds unnecessary visual complexity — decorative backgrounds, artistic flourishes, multiple competing elements. You can explicitly exclude these with negative prompts using the --no parameter.
steps.code:
Add to the end of your prompt:

'--no color backgrounds, decorative elements, artistic borders, shadows, gradients'

Full example:
'Diagram of the nitrogen cycle showing all major stages, flat educational illustration style, white background, labelled --no artistic flourishes, decorative borders, gradients, photorealism'
steps.tip: White background + labelled + flat illustration style eliminates most of the common issues with AI-generated diagrams for classroom use. Make these your default constraints.

steps.title: Use aspect ratio flags for presentation use
steps.content: By default, Midjourney generates square images. For classroom presentations (16:9 slide format) or A4 print materials, specify the aspect ratio.
steps.code:
Common flags:

'--ar 16:9' — for presentation slides (widescreen)
'--ar 4:3' — for older projector formats
'--ar 1:1' — for square social media or print use
'--ar 3:4' — for portrait print materials (A4-ish)

Full example:
'Timeline of the Indian independence movement, key events labelled, flat illustration style, horizontal layout --ar 16:9 --no decorative borders, shadows'

steps.title: Know what requires a different tool
steps.content: Midjourney cannot reliably produce accurate complex text labels within images, precise multi-step flowcharts, or diagrams where specific positioning matters (like circuit diagrams or precise anatomical detail). For those tasks, use a purpose-built tool instead.
steps.code:
Use Midjourney for: conceptual illustrations, historical scenes, portraits, conceptual diagrams, atmosphere-setting images

Use a different tool for:
- Precise flowcharts with exact positioning → draw.io, Lucidchart, or Mermaid
- Accurate anatomical diagrams → BioRender (free for education)
- Data visualisations → Google Charts, Canva
- Maps with precise geography → Google Maps screenshots, MapChart
steps.warning: Text in Midjourney images is notoriously unreliable. Even when you ask for specific labels, the text is often garbled or misspelled. If labels matter for accuracy, generate the base diagram in Midjourney and add text manually in Canva or PowerPoint.

walkthroughs.title: Gemini in Google Docs and Sheets: practical workflows
walkthroughs.description: Gemini is built into Google Workspace. If you already live in Docs and Sheets, Gemini is the AI tool with the lowest friction — you don't switch apps, you don't copy-paste, you work where you already are. This walkthrough covers the integrations worth using.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Gemini's advantage is context. In Docs, it can work on your actual document. In Sheets, it can reason about your actual data. No copy-paste, no context translation.

steps.title: Access Gemini in Google Docs
steps.content: Open any Google Doc. Look for the Gemini icon (a star/sparkle) in the right sidebar or at the bottom of the document. If it's not visible, check that your Google account has Gemini enabled — it requires a Google Workspace account or Google One AI Premium subscription.
steps.tip: The 'Help me write' prompt appears at the start of a blank document. For existing documents, use the sidebar to ask questions or generate additions without disrupting your existing content.

steps.title: Use Gemini to work on your existing document
steps.content: Highlight a section of your document, then use the Gemini sidebar. It can see the content you've selected and work on it directly — summarise it, rewrite it for a different audience, extend it, or check it against something.
steps.code:
In a lesson plan document:
- Select the learning objectives section → ask Gemini to 'rewrite these objectives in student-facing language'
- Select an explanation → ask it to 'simplify this for a student with limited English'
- Select a section → ask 'what's missing from this that a complete lesson plan should include?'

In meeting notes or a school policy document:
- Select the full document → ask 'summarise the key decisions and action items'
- Select a paragraph → ask 'what does this mean in practical terms?'

steps.title: Use Gemini in Google Sheets for data tasks
steps.content: In Sheets, Gemini can look at your actual data. Select a range of cells, open the Gemini sidebar, and ask questions about the data — or ask it to generate formulas. This is significantly more useful than explaining your data structure to a separate AI tool.
steps.code:
Practical Sheets uses for educators:

'I have student grades in columns B through H. Write a formula to calculate each student's average and highlight any average below 40%.'

'This column contains parent contact information in inconsistent formats. Write a formula to extract just the phone numbers.'

'I have attendance data for 30 students over 20 days. Write a formula to calculate each student's attendance percentage and flag anyone below 75%.'
steps.tip: Ask Gemini to explain the formula it generates before you use it. Understanding what it does helps you catch errors and adapt it when your data changes.

steps.title: What Gemini in Workspace can't do reliably
steps.content: Gemini's Workspace integration is powerful for tasks that stay within your documents, but it has real limitations worth knowing before you rely on it.
steps.code:
Limitations to know:

- It doesn't reliably access all files in your Drive by default — it works on what's currently open or what you explicitly share with it
- It can make formula errors in complex Sheets tasks — always test on sample data before applying broadly
- In Docs, 'Help me write' generates at a quality level below ChatGPT or Claude for most writing tasks — treat it as a starting point, not a final draft
- It can't access external sources in the Workspace integration — for research tasks, use Gemini.google.com separately
steps.warning: Gemini in Workspace sends your document content to Google's servers for processing. For documents containing sensitive student data (grades, personal information), check your school's data privacy policy before using AI features on those files.

walkthroughs.title: Your first AI-generated design in under 5 minutes
walkthroughs.description: Canva AI removes the blank-page problem. You describe what you need and it produces a working starting point — then you edit. This walkthrough gets you to your first usable design and teaches you what to change and what to leave alone.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Canva AI is a starting-point engine, not a finishing engine. Its strength is eliminating the blank canvas; your job is editing the output into something accurate and appropriate for your audience.

steps.title: Go to Canva and open the AI tools
steps.content: Go to canva.com and create a free account. From the homepage, click 'Create a design'. You'll see template suggestions — ignore these for now. Instead, look for 'Magic Design' in the left sidebar under the AI tools section, or type what you need in the search bar and look for the 'Generate with AI' option that appears alongside templates.
steps.tip: If you're an educator, register at canva.com/education for Canva for Education — the free tier gives you access to premium features including AI tools that are paywalled for regular free accounts. Verification takes under a minute with a school email address.

steps.title: Describe what you need — specifically
steps.content: In the Magic Design prompt field, describe the design you need. Be specific about: the format (poster, presentation, worksheet, infographic), the topic, the audience, and the purpose. Vague prompts produce generic designs that need more editing.
steps.code:
Vague: 'Science poster'

Specific: 'A4 classroom poster explaining the water cycle for Class 6 students, with space for a labelled diagram, key vocabulary terms, and two reflection questions. Clean, colourful design appropriate for a school wall.'

Another example:
'Single-page student worksheet on photosynthesis for Class 7. Include a blank diagram to label, five fill-in-the-blank sentences, and three short-answer questions. Minimalist design, easy to print in black and white.'
steps.tip: Include the output format (A4, A3, 16:9 slide), the age group, and whether it needs to be print-friendly. These three constraints eliminate most of the common generation failures.

steps.title: Choose the best starting point from the generated options
steps.content: Canva AI generates multiple layout options. Don't select the most visually impressive one — select the one closest to the structure you actually need. You'll be editing the content anyway; what you can't easily change is the fundamental layout. Prefer simpler, cleaner layouts over busy ones.
steps.tip: The AI-generated images inside Canva designs are placeholders that you can swap. Text content is almost always wrong and needs replacing — treat everything as editable. Choose your starting point based on layout and structure, not on whether the placeholder content is accurate.

steps.title: Edit the content — don't use the AI text as-is
steps.content: Click any text element to edit it directly. The AI-generated text is a structural placeholder — it may be factually wrong, too generic, or pitched at the wrong level. Replace it with your own accurate content. This is the step most beginners skip, and it is why AI-generated classroom materials sometimes contain errors.
steps.warning: AI-generated text inside Canva designs is produced for layout demonstration, not for factual accuracy. Science definitions, historical facts, and curriculum-specific content should be replaced with content you have verified. Never share an AI-designed educational resource without reading every word of text in it.

steps.title: Download in the right format
steps.content: Click 'Share' then 'Download'. For print materials: PDF Print (highest quality). For digital sharing: PNG or JPEG for single images, PDF Standard for multi-page documents. For presentations: PDF or use the 'Present' mode directly in Canva.
steps.code:
Download format guide:

For printing at school: PDF Print
For sharing on WhatsApp or email: PNG (single page) or PDF Standard
For Google Classroom upload: PDF Standard
For display on a screen/projector: PNG or use Canva Present mode
For editing later: save as Canva file (stays in your account automatically)
steps.tip: For worksheets you will print multiple times: download as PDF Print once and store it. Re-downloading every time creates unnecessary file versions.

walkthroughs.title: Magic Design: turning a topic into a full presentation
walkthroughs.description: Magic Design can take a topic — or even a document you upload — and generate a full multi-slide presentation with layout, imagery, and placeholder text. For educators who need to produce professional-looking slides quickly, this is the highest-ROI use of Canva AI. This walkthrough covers the workflow and the critical editing steps that turn an AI draft into a presentation you would actually show a class.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Magic Design gives you structure and visual design in under 60 seconds. Your job is content accuracy, sequence logic, and audience calibration — the three things AI gets wrong most often in presentations.

steps.title: Start from a prompt or from a document
steps.content: From the Canva homepage, click 'Presentation' then 'Magic Design'. You'll see two options: type a topic prompt, or upload a document (PDF, Word, or text file). For educators: the document upload path often produces better-structured decks because the AI has actual content to work from, not just a topic name.
steps.code:
Prompt approach (for a new topic):
'15-slide presentation for Class 9 students on the Indian independence movement. Include key dates, major figures, important events from 1857 to 1947, and two discussion questions. Clean, educational design.'

Document approach (for existing material):
Upload your lesson notes, a textbook chapter, or a handout and Magic Design extracts the structure and builds slides from it.
steps.tip: If you're using the prompt approach, specifying the number of slides forces the AI to distribute content more thoughtfully. Without a slide count, it tends to over-compress or produce slides that are too text-heavy.

steps.title: Select a theme that suits your context
steps.content: After the initial generation, Canva shows your slides in multiple visual themes. For classroom use: choose themes with high contrast, large text, and minimal decorative clutter. Avoid dark backgrounds unless you are certain of projector quality — many school projectors wash out dark themes significantly.
steps.tip: After choosing a theme, you can swap it at any time using the 'Design' panel on the right. Changing the theme doesn't reset your content edits — only your font and colour choices. It's safe to experiment with themes late in the editing process.

steps.title: Fix the three things AI gets wrong in presentations
steps.content: AI-generated presentations consistently fail in the same three ways. Fix each one before sharing.
steps.code:
Problem 1: Content accuracy
The AI fills slides with plausible-sounding content that may be factually wrong. Read every slide for accuracy — especially dates, names, and quoted statistics.

Problem 2: Sequence logic
AI arranges slides in a reasonable order, not necessarily a pedagogically effective one. Ask: does each slide build on the previous one?

Problem 3: Text density
AI-generated slides are almost always too text-heavy. A readable classroom slide has a maximum of 30 words. Cut everything that is not essential — the rest belongs in your verbal delivery.
steps.warning: Do not present an AI-generated slide deck without reading through it slide by slide, out loud. It is the only way to catch all three failure modes. Reading silently misses the verbal logic gaps.

steps.title: Replace AI images with appropriate ones
steps.content: Click any AI-generated image on a slide. In the left panel, you can: search Canva's stock photo library (mostly free), upload your own images, or use Canva's AI image generator to create something specific. For educational use, stick to stock photos or illustrations where accuracy isn't critical — for scientific diagrams, create them separately.
steps.tip: Search Canva's library with specific, simple terms: 'water cycle diagram', 'Indian village market', 'microscope illustration'. Canva's library is large enough that specific searches often return exactly what you need without using the AI generator.

walkthroughs.title: Building a classroom resource kit with Canva AI
walkthroughs.description: Rather than creating individual materials one at a time, Canva AI lets you build an entire visual resource kit for a unit — matching worksheets, posters, presentation slides, and assessment materials — with consistent design across all of them. This walkthrough shows how to do that efficiently.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Consistency and speed come from setting up a Brand Kit once and letting every subsequent resource inherit from it — rather than re-designing from scratch each time.

steps.title: Set up a simple Brand Kit for your classroom
steps.content: Go to Brand Hub in the left sidebar (available with Canva for Education). Create a brand kit with: your school colours (or a consistent two-colour palette), one heading font and one body font, and your school logo if you have it. Every resource you create after this can inherit these settings in one click.
steps.code:
Suggested simple classroom brand kit:

Primary colour: your school colour OR a subject colour code
  (e.g. blue for science, green for biology, red for maths)
Secondary colour: white or light grey for backgrounds
Heading font: Poppins Bold or Montserrat Bold (clean and readable)
Body font: Open Sans or Lato (readable at small sizes)
Logo: school crest or department name as a text logo
steps.tip: Even without a school logo, a consistent colour and font pair makes your materials look professionally designed. Students recognise and associate materials from the same teacher — it helps with engagement and organisation.

steps.title: Build the kit piece by piece using Magic Design
steps.content: For a single unit, generate in sequence: one classroom poster, a student reference card, a worksheet, and a summary slide deck. Use your brand kit colours to give the whole kit a consistent feel.
steps.code:
Prompt sequence for a Photosynthesis unit kit:

1. Poster: 'A3 classroom poster on photosynthesis. Key equation, labelled diagram, light vs dark reactions. Educational illustration style.'

2. Reference card: 'A5 student quick-reference card on photosynthesis. Key terms, the equation, and a simplified diagram.'

3. Worksheet: 'A4 student worksheet on photosynthesis. Blank diagram to label, matching exercise, and three short-answer questions. Print-friendly.'

4. Slides: '12-slide Class 8 lesson on photosynthesis. One concept per slide. Include a recap slide and a check-for-understanding question slide.'

steps.title: Use folders to organise by unit and year
steps.content: In Canva, create a folder for each teaching unit. Store all related materials together. At the end of the year, duplicate the folder and refresh for next year — updating only what changed. This compounds over time: your third year of using Canva produces resources much faster than your first year.
steps.tip: Name your designs clearly: 'Class 8 Science - Photosynthesis - Poster - 2025' rather than 'Untitled Design 47'. Canva's search function makes retrievable what you name correctly.

steps.title: Share with students and parents directly from Canva
steps.content: Finished materials can be shared as a link (view-only), embedded in Google Classroom, downloaded as PDF, or shared directly to WhatsApp from Canva mobile.
steps.warning: If you share a Canva link rather than a downloaded PDF, students can see the full design including any unlocked layers. For worksheets with answer keys on a separate layer, always download and share the PDF — not the live Canva link.

walkthroughs.title: Generate a full presentation from a single prompt
walkthroughs.description: Gamma was built specifically for one purpose: making the generation of structured, well-designed presentations fast. Unlike Canva or PowerPoint where design and content are separate problems, Gamma handles both simultaneously from a single natural language prompt. This walkthrough shows you what that looks like in practice and what the real limitations are.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Gamma's output quality is proportional to the structure of your input. A structured outline produces a structured deck. A vague sentence produces something you'll spend 30 minutes fixing.

steps.title: Open Gamma and choose your generation mode
steps.content: Go to gamma.app and sign up for a free account. Click 'New AI'. You'll see three options: Generate (from a prompt), Paste in text (from existing notes or an outline), and Import (from a file). For your first use, start with Generate.
steps.tip: The free Gamma account gives you a limited number of AI credits per month. Generating from pasted text uses fewer credits and often produces better results because your structure is driving the output.

steps.title: Write a structured prompt — not just a topic
steps.content: The most important skill in using Gamma is front-loading structure into your prompt. If you give Gamma a structured outline, it produces a structured deck.
steps.code:
Weak prompt:
'Climate change for school students'

Strong prompt:
'Presentation for Class 10 students on climate change. Structure: (1) What is the greenhouse effect — 2 slides. (2) Evidence — 2 slides with data. (3) Impact on India — 2 slides. (4) What students can do — 2 slides. (5) One closing discussion question. Keep language accessible, use Indian examples where possible.'

Even better — paste an outline directly into the text input mode.
steps.tip: Specifying the number of slides per section forces Gamma to distribute content appropriately. Without this, it packs too much into some slides and too little into others.

steps.title: Review and edit inside Gamma's editor
steps.content: Once generated, Gamma opens the full deck in its editor. Each card is independently editable. Click any text to edit it. Click the AI button within a card to ask Gamma to rewrite, expand, simplify, or restructure that specific card.
steps.code:
Useful in-card AI commands:
'Simplify this for a 14-year-old reader'
'Add a real-world Indian example to illustrate this point'
'Convert this text into 3 bullet points'
'Rewrite this as a question for class discussion'
'Add a statistic that supports this claim' (always verify the statistic it adds)
steps.warning: When you ask Gamma to 'add a statistic', it will generate a plausible-sounding number that may not be accurate. Always search for the statistic it produces before presenting it as fact.

steps.title: Share, present, or export
steps.content: From the top right, you can: present in full-screen directly from Gamma (no download needed), share a public link for students to view at their own pace, export to PDF, or export to PowerPoint format.
steps.tip: The 'Share as link' option is the highest-value Gamma feature for educators. Students can view the presentation on their phone without downloading anything. You can update the deck after sharing — the link always shows the current version.

walkthroughs.title: Using Gamma for student project presentations
walkthroughs.description: Gamma lowers the barrier to producing a professional-looking presentation so far that students who previously submitted hand-drawn charts or plain text documents can produce something genuinely polished. This walkthrough covers how to set up a student Gamma workflow — and the critical teaching point about AI-assisted work that educators need to address explicitly.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Gamma changes the presentation skill floor — any student can produce a polished deck. What you need to explicitly assess is the quality of thought, not the quality of the design.

steps.title: Why Gamma works well for student projects
steps.content: Traditional presentation tools penalise students who are less design-savvy — a student with good ideas but poor PowerPoint skills consistently produces weaker-looking work. Gamma removes that inequity: design quality is no longer a differentiating factor.
steps.tip: Before assigning Gamma-based presentations, update your rubric to explicitly weight content, argument quality, and evidence use — and explicitly de-weight visual design. Otherwise students and teachers will unconsciously reward visual polish over intellectual substance.

steps.title: Set up the assignment with clear AI-use boundaries
steps.content: Before students start, establish what AI-assistance is permitted and what is not. Gamma can generate both structure and content — which means a student could produce an entire presentation without engaging with the material at all.
steps.code:
Example assignment parameters:

Permitted:
- Using Gamma to generate an initial slide structure from their own written outline
- Using AI to reformat or clean up text they wrote
- Using AI image generation for decorative visuals

Not permitted:
- Using AI to write the content of the slides
- Using AI to generate the argument or thesis
- Presenting AI-generated statistics without verifying and citing them

Required:
- Submit the original written outline used to generate the deck
- Every factual claim must have a cited source in the speaker notes

steps.title: Walk students through the generation-then-edit workflow
steps.content: The most common student mistake: accepting the AI generation without editing. Teach the workflow explicitly: the AI generation is a starting structure, not a finished product.
steps.code:
Teach this workflow:

1. Write your own outline on paper or in a doc — do not start in Gamma
2. Paste your outline into Gamma and generate
3. For each card: read the AI-generated text and ask whether it is accurate and specific
4. Replace generic AI content with specific evidence, examples, or arguments from your research
5. In speaker notes: write what you will actually say about each slide
steps.tip: The speaker notes field is the best diagnostic for whether a student engaged with the material. AI-generated speaker notes are recognisably generic. Student-written speaker notes reflecting genuine understanding are quite different in quality and specificity.

walkthroughs.title: Gamma vs PowerPoint vs Canva: honest comparison for educators
walkthroughs.description: Three very different tools that all produce slide decks. The right choice depends on what you are optimising for. This walkthrough gives you an honest, task-specific comparison so you stop defaulting to PowerPoint for everything.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Default to Gamma when speed matters most. Default to Canva when visual creativity matters most. Default to PowerPoint only when you need compatibility with a system that requires it.

steps.title: When to use Gamma
steps.content: Gamma is the right tool when: you need a presentation in under 15 minutes, you're working from notes or an outline, you want something professional without design work, or you need a shareable link rather than a file.
steps.code:
Best use cases:
- Weekly lesson recap decks
- Professional development presentations
- Student project presentations
- Quick explainer decks for parents or admin
- Any presentation where you are the subject expert and just need design help

steps.title: When to use Canva
steps.content: Canva is the right tool when: visual design quality is important, you need materials beyond slides (worksheets, posters), you want more control over layout, or you're creating materials that will be printed.
steps.code:
Best use cases:
- Classroom posters and display materials
- Student-facing worksheets
- School communications and newsletters
- Presentations that need custom branded design
- Materials where visual accuracy matters

steps.title: When to use PowerPoint
steps.content: PowerPoint is the right tool when: you need compatibility with your school's existing systems, you're collaborating with colleagues who use it, you need complex animations, or you're submitting to an institution that requires .pptx format.
steps.code:
Best use cases:
- Formal institutional submissions
- When your school system requires .pptx
- Complex animations not possible in Gamma
- Real-time co-editing with a colleague
- Existing presentations you have built over years

steps.title: The hybrid workflow that works best
steps.content: Many educators find the most efficient workflow is using them in sequence. Generate the structure in Gamma. Export to PowerPoint. Refine in PowerPoint or import to Canva for additional polish.
steps.tip: Gamma's PowerPoint export preserves layout and text reasonably well but loses some formatting. Treat the export as an editable starting point, not a finished product.

walkthroughs.title: Gen-3: your first AI video from a text prompt
walkthroughs.description: Runway Gen-3 generates short video clips from a text description. The output is not a finished classroom video; it is a raw clip that can be used as part of a larger presentation, explainer, or creative project. This walkthrough shows you what to expect, how to prompt well, and what not to try.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Runway generates atmospheric and conceptual clips well. It generates precise, factually accurate, or instructional clips poorly. Match your task to what the tool actually does.

steps.title: Set up Runway and understand the free tier
steps.content: Go to runwayml.com and create a free account. The free tier gives you a limited number of generation credits. Each video generation uses credits — plan before you generate rather than experimenting freely.
steps.tip: Use the free tier to learn what kinds of prompts produce useful output in your subject area. Once you understand the prompt patterns that work, your generation efficiency improves significantly.

steps.title: Write a video prompt with the right structure
steps.content: A Runway prompt describes: the subject, the setting, the camera movement, and the mood or style. The more cinematic your description, the better the output.
steps.code:
Prompt structure:
[Subject and action] [Setting and context] [Camera movement] [Style/mood]

Examples:

'A time-lapse of a seed germinating and growing into a plant, close-up macro shot, soft natural lighting, scientific documentary style'

'Water flowing over rocks in a mountain stream, slow motion, aerial shot slowly descending, peaceful and serene'

'Cells dividing under a microscope, extreme close-up, scientific visualization style, blue and white colour palette'
steps.tip: Camera movement terms that work reliably: 'slow zoom in', 'aerial shot descending', 'tracking shot', 'timelapse', 'slow motion', 'static camera'. Include one movement instruction per prompt.
