steps.title: Generate and evaluate your first clip
steps.content: Select Gen-3 Alpha from the generation options, paste your prompt, and click Generate. Clips take 30 to 90 seconds to generate. Watch it once for general quality, then again specifically for visual errors.
steps.warning: Runway clips almost always contain visual artifacts — elements that morph strangely, backgrounds that shift, or objects that move unnaturally. This is a fundamental characteristic of current AI video, not a prompt error. The question is whether the artifacts are distracting enough to make the clip unusable.

steps.title: Use clips as supporting visuals, not as standalone content
steps.content: The most practical educational use of Runway clips is as background or atmospheric visuals in a larger presentation — playing silently behind a voiceover, as a visual hook at the start of a lesson, or as a creative stimulus.
steps.code:
Good educational uses:

'Opening hook': a 5-second atmospheric clip signalling a topic — plays silently while you introduce the lesson

'Creative stimulus': show a surreal clip and ask students what it represents

'Writing prompt': show a landscape clip and ask students to write a story or description

'Background visuals': use as a looping background during group work or transitions
steps.tip: For factual educational content — how photosynthesis works, how the heart pumps blood — use verified scientific animation from sources like Khan Academy or TED-Ed. Use Runway only for atmospheric visuals.

walkthroughs.title: Ethics and responsibility in AI video generation
walkthroughs.description: AI video generation is the most ethically consequential tool on this list. The ability to create photorealistic video of things that never happened creates risks that do not exist with text or image AI tools. This walkthrough is about what every user of AI video tools must understand before sharing anything they generate.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: The most important question before sharing any AI-generated video is: could this be mistaken for real footage? If the answer is yes or maybe, it must be labelled clearly as AI-generated before you share it.

steps.title: Why AI video is different from AI text and images
steps.content: AI video can now produce footage that looks like real recorded events — and humans are poorly calibrated to distinguish AI video from genuine footage, especially at normal viewing speeds. This asymmetry creates responsibilities that other AI tools do not.
steps.tip: Even short, low-stakes clips should carry an AI disclosure. Normalising the habit of labelling all AI-generated video is more protective than trying to decide case-by-case which clips need labelling.

steps.title: What you must never generate
steps.content: Runway's terms of service and basic ethical obligations prohibit certain content regardless of your intent.
steps.code:
Never generate:
- Realistic footage of real, named, living people
- Footage designed to look like genuine news or documentary footage of real events
- Content that could spread false information about real people or organisations
- Violent or graphic content
- Footage of minors in any realistic or suggestive context

For educators specifically:
- Never generate footage that looks like real students, school events, or classroom situations
- Do not use AI video as a substitute for real documentary evidence or historical footage without clearly distinguishing what is real and what is generated

steps.title: Label everything — always
steps.content: Any AI-generated video clip you share must be clearly labelled as AI-generated before sharing. This applies to educational materials, social media posts, school presentations, and WhatsApp messages.
steps.code:
Label formats:

In a presentation slide: add text overlay 'AI-generated video — not real footage' in the first 2 seconds

In a document: caption reads 'Created using AI (Runway ML) — not real footage'

In social media: write 'AI-generated' in the post text before the video

For student assignments: require label 'Created using Runway AI — not original footage'
steps.warning: Sharing AI-generated video without labelling it as AI-generated is ethically wrong even when the content is harmless. It normalises unlabelled synthetic media and erodes the viewer's ability to trust any video they encounter.

steps.title: Teach students to spot AI video — not just create it
steps.content: The most valuable AI video lesson for students is not how to use Runway. It is developing the habit of questioning whether video they encounter was AI-generated.
steps.code:
Signs of AI-generated video (current generation):
- Unnatural motion at edges of objects
- Hands and fingers that distort or have incorrect numbers of digits
- Text in the video that is blurry, shifting, or misspelled
- Backgrounds that change subtly between frames
- Lighting that does not match between foreground and background

Classroom activity: show students 5 clips — some real, some AI-generated. Ask them to identify which is which and explain their reasoning.
steps.tip: The goal is not to make students paranoid about all video — it is to develop a calibrated reflex: for anything consequential, verify provenance before accepting or sharing.

walkthroughs.title: What makes Consensus different from Google Scholar
walkthroughs.description: Google Scholar finds papers. Consensus reads them and tells you what they found. Finding a relevant paper is one skill; extracting and synthesising its conclusions is another. Consensus automates the second step, which is usually the harder one.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Use Google Scholar to find specific papers you already know about. Use Consensus to answer questions about what the evidence says — when you do not yet know which papers matter.

steps.title: What Consensus actually does
steps.content: Go to consensus.app and sign up for a free account. When you search a question, Consensus searches peer-reviewed academic papers, identifies the relevant ones, extracts the key findings, and synthesises them into a direct answer with citations. It does not summarise the internet — it summarises the academic literature specifically.
steps.tip: The free tier of Consensus gives you a limited number of AI-powered Consensus Meter results per month. The basic search (finding papers and showing their key findings) is unlimited. Learn to extract value from the paper results directly before relying on the AI synthesis.

steps.title: Ask a research question, not a keyword
steps.content: Consensus is designed for questions, not keyword searches. The difference in output quality is significant.
steps.code:
Google Scholar approach (keyword):
'spaced repetition learning'

Consensus approach (question):
'Does spaced repetition improve long-term retention compared to massed practice?'

More examples:
'Is homework associated with better academic outcomes in secondary school students?'

'What are the most effective interventions for improving reading comprehension in early primary school?'

'Does class size affect student achievement in developing countries?'
steps.tip: Consensus works best with empirical questions — does X affect Y? or is X associated with Z? It is less effective for theoretical or historical questions.

steps.title: Read the Consensus Meter — and understand its limits
steps.content: On many searches, Consensus shows a Consensus Meter — a visual indicator of whether the evidence broadly supports, refutes, or is mixed on your question. This is useful as a starting signal, but requires careful interpretation.
steps.code:
How to read the Consensus Meter accurately:

'Strongly supports': Multiple papers with consistent findings — but check whether they study the same population and context as yours

'Mixed results': The evidence genuinely varies — dig into WHY it varies

'Insufficient evidence': Few papers on this topic — be cautious about strong claims

What the Meter does not tell you:
- Quality of the papers (small studies count the same as large ones)
- Recency of the evidence
- Whether the context matches your situation
steps.warning: A 'strongly supports' Consensus Meter result does not mean the claim is proven. It means Consensus found multiple papers pointing in the same direction. Publication bias, small sample sizes, and context-specificity all limit what you can conclude.

walkthroughs.title: Using Consensus for literature reviews and research papers
walkthroughs.description: A literature review requires finding relevant papers, understanding what each says, identifying where they agree and disagree, and synthesising a coherent picture of the field. Consensus can significantly accelerate steps one and two — but it cannot replace the critical thinking required for steps three and four.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Consensus accelerates the scoping and paper identification phase of a literature review. The analysis, synthesis, and argument-building still require your own thinking.

steps.title: Use Consensus to scope the field first
steps.content: Before diving into individual papers, use Consensus to map the landscape. Search your core question and pay attention to the range of findings and paper titles. This gives you a rapid overview of how much research exists, what the main variables are, and whether the field has clear consensus or genuine debate.
steps.code:
Opening scoping questions:

'What is the relationship between [your variable A] and [your variable B]?'

'What factors influence [your outcome of interest]?'

'What interventions have been shown to improve [your outcome]?'

From the results, note:
- Which specific definitions appear consistently?
- What populations are most studied?
- Are there obvious gaps in the literature?

steps.title: Save and organise the most relevant papers
steps.content: When you find relevant papers, click through to the original source and read the abstract directly. Do not rely on Consensus summary alone — a paper that sounds relevant from the extraction may study a slightly different population or variable than you need.
steps.tip: Use Zotero (free reference manager) to save papers you find in Consensus. Add a tag for each paper indicating how you found it and its relevance level. This makes your literature review process auditable.

steps.title: Use specific sub-questions to map disagreements
steps.content: When the evidence is mixed, use Consensus to probe the sub-questions. The pattern of differences across them often explains why the broad question shows mixed results.
steps.code:
From broad to specific:

Broad: 'Does homework improve academic performance?'
→ Mixed results

Probing the disagreement:
'Does homework improve performance for primary school students?'
'Does homework improve performance for secondary school students?'
'Do homework effects vary by socioeconomic status?'

Each sub-question produces a more specific evidence picture.

steps.title: What Consensus cannot do for a literature review
steps.content: Be explicit with yourself about the tasks that remain yours, regardless of how useful Consensus has been for scoping.
steps.code:
Consensus cannot:

- Assess methodological quality of individual papers — you must read the methods section
- Tell you which papers are most authoritative — you need to check citation counts and journal quality
- Synthesise papers that disagree — you must read both and reason about why they conflict
- Update you on papers published in the last few months — its index has a lag
- Replace your argument — Consensus shows what papers say; your review argues why it matters
steps.warning: Do not cite a paper in your literature review based solely on Consensus extraction. Read the abstract and the relevant sections of the paper directly. Every citation in your review should be based on your direct reading of the source.

walkthroughs.title: Teaching students to evaluate research quality with Consensus
walkthroughs.description: Most students have never been taught to evaluate whether a piece of research is trustworthy. Consensus provides a practical classroom tool for teaching research literacy — because it surfaces real papers, real findings, and real disagreements in a format accessible to secondary and tertiary students.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Consensus is the first research tool most students have used that shows them the evidence base directly, rather than a journalist or influencer's interpretation of it. That shift in contact with evidence is itself the lesson.

steps.title: Start with a question students actually have opinions on
steps.content: The best Consensus classroom activities start with a question students think they already know the answer to. The contrast between their assumption and the actual evidence is where learning happens.
steps.code:
Questions that work well:

'Does listening to music while studying improve academic performance?'
'Is breakfast really the most important meal of the day for school performance?'
'Do smaller class sizes lead to better student outcomes?'
'Does social media use harm mental health in teenagers?'
'Is learning a second language easier for children than adults?'

Before searching: ask students to write down what they believe the evidence shows and how confident they are. Then search together and compare.

steps.title: Teach the three questions to ask about any paper
steps.content: When Consensus surfaces a paper, teach students to ask three questions before accepting its finding as relevant.
steps.code:
The three evaluation questions:

1. 'Who did they study?' (Is this population similar to the situation we are asking about? A study of US university students may not apply to Class 10 students in India.)

2. 'How many people did they study?' (A study of 40 people is much weaker evidence than a study of 4,000 people.)

3. 'How did they measure the outcome?' (If the outcome is 'academic performance', did they measure exam scores, grades, or teacher ratings? These are different things.)
steps.tip: These three questions do not require any statistics knowledge. Any student who can read can learn to ask them. Teach them as a transferable habit for every piece of research they encounter.

steps.title: Run a 'consensus vs claim' fact-check activity
steps.content: Take a specific claim from a news article or social media post that students encounter regularly. Use Consensus to check whether the academic evidence supports that claim.
steps.code:
Activity structure:

1. Show students the claim (e.g. a headline: 'Study shows homework is harmful to children')
2. Ask: what question would we search in Consensus to check this?
3. Search together and review the evidence
4. Ask: does the evidence support the specific claim in the headline? Why or why not?
5. Discuss: what might have been lost or exaggerated between the original research and the headline?
steps.warning: Some topics students might want to search will surface real academic papers with frank clinical content. Preview any Consensus search before showing results to a class, particularly with younger students.

walkthroughs.title: Your first program: from zero to running code in 10 minutes
walkthroughs.description: Most people who want to learn coding give up before they write a single line — because setup is hard. Replit eliminates setup entirely. You open a browser, pick a language, and start writing. This walkthrough gets you to your first working Python program without installing anything, and introduces Replit AI as the tool you will use to learn from what goes wrong.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: The goal of your first program is not to build something impressive. It is to complete the write-run-see loop once. Once you have done it, you understand the fundamental cycle of programming — and everything after that is elaboration.

steps.title: Create your first Repl
steps.content: Go to replit.com and create a free account. Click '+ Create Repl'. Choose Python as your language. Give it a name. Click 'Create Repl'. You now have a code editor on the left and a terminal/output panel on the right.
steps.tip: If you're a teacher setting up for students: Replit Teams for Education is free for educators and gives you a shared workspace where you can see student code, leave comments, and set exercises.

steps.title: Write your first line of code — and run it
steps.content: In the code editor, click to place your cursor and type the following exactly as written:
steps.code: print("Hello, world!")
steps.tip: Now click the green 'Run' button at the top. In the right-hand panel, you should see: Hello, world! — If you do: you've written and run your first program. The write-run-see loop is the fundamental unit of all programming.

steps.title: Make it yours — and make it break
steps.content: Change the text inside the quotation marks to something else. Run it again. Now try deleting one of the quotation marks and running it. Read the error message carefully.
steps.code:
What breaking looks like:
print("Hello, world!)

Error you will see:
SyntaxError: EOL while scanning string literal

What this means:
Python reached the end of the line while still looking for the closing quotation mark.
steps.warning: Error messages are not failures — they are information. The goal of the breaking exercise is to establish a habit: when code breaks, read the error message before doing anything else. The message almost always tells you exactly what went wrong and where.

steps.title: Use Replit AI to understand the error
steps.content: In Replit, click the AI button in the left sidebar. When your code produces an error, paste the error message and ask Replit AI to explain it. This is the core learning workflow: write, get an error, ask AI to explain the error, understand it, fix it, repeat.
steps.code:
Ask Replit AI:
'I got this error: SyntaxError: EOL while scanning string literal on line 1. Can you explain what this means and what I probably did wrong?'

What Replit AI does:
It reads your code and the error, explains the problem in plain language, and usually shows you the corrected version. Read both the explanation AND the corrected code.
steps.tip: Don't paste the error into AI and copy the fix without reading the explanation. The fix solves today's error. The explanation prevents tomorrow's. Develop the habit of reading both every single time.

steps.title: Write a program that asks for your name
steps.content: Now build a slightly more complex program — one that takes input from the user and responds to it. This introduces variables and user input.
steps.code:
name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Hello, " + name + "! Welcome to Python.")

What each line does:
Line 1: input() shows the text, waits for the user to type something, and stores it in a variable called name
Line 2: print() outputs text — the + signs join three pieces of text together
steps.tip: Variables are storage boxes. 'name' is a box that holds whatever the user typed. You can use the variable name anywhere in your program and it will be replaced by its contents.

walkthroughs.title: Debugging: how to use AI to understand what went wrong
walkthroughs.description: Every programmer spends more time debugging than writing new code. The difference between a programmer who gets better and one who gets frustrated and quits is almost entirely in how they respond to errors. This walkthrough teaches the debugging workflow that turns errors from obstacles into lessons.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Debugging is not an interruption to learning programming — it IS learning programming. Every error is a precise description of a misconception you had. Reading errors carefully is the fastest way to close knowledge gaps.

steps.title: The three-step debugging reflex
steps.content: Before touching your code after an error, complete these three steps in order. This prevents the most common debugging failure: making random changes until something works, without understanding why.
steps.code:
Step 1: READ the error message — full text, not just the first line
Step 2: LOCATE the line number it mentions — go to that exact line
Step 3: UNDERSTAND what Python expected vs what it found

Only then: fix the code.

If you skip to fixing without understanding, you will make the same error again. The error message tells you exactly what Python expected. Understanding that expectation is the knowledge you are building.

steps.title: Common errors and what they actually mean
steps.content: Python's error messages are written for programmers, not beginners. Here is a plain-language translation of the ones you will encounter most often.
steps.code:
SyntaxError: invalid syntax
Meaning: Python could not parse this line — usually a missing bracket, colon, or quotation mark

NameError: name 'x' is not defined
Meaning: you used a variable name that Python has not seen yet
Look for: typos in variable names, or using a variable before you assigned it

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not 'int') to str
Meaning: you tried to join text with a number without converting
Fix: use str() to convert the number first

IndexError: list index out of range
Meaning: you asked for an item that does not exist in the list

IndentationError: expected an indented block
Meaning: Python uses indentation to define code blocks — you have the wrong number of spaces

steps.title: Ask Replit AI the right question
steps.content: When you use Replit AI for debugging, the quality of your question determines the quality of the explanation. The best questions include: the error message, the line it came from, and what you expected the code to do.
steps.code:
Weak question to AI:
'Why is my code broken?'

Strong question to AI:
'My code is supposed to print the average of a list of numbers. I get this error: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: int and str on line 6. Here is my code: [paste code]. Can you explain what is wrong and why?'

What makes it strong:
- States the intended behaviour
- Pastes the full error message
- Includes the specific line number
- Pastes the relevant code
- Asks for an explanation, not just a fix
steps.tip: After Replit AI explains the fix, type the correction yourself — do not copy-paste it. The physical act of typing the corrected code reinforces the pattern. Copy-pasting working code teaches you nothing about why it works.

steps.title: Keep an error log — make your mistakes useful
steps.content: Start a simple text file in Replit called errors.txt. Every time you encounter a new error type, write it down with: the error name, what caused it, and what you did to fix it.
steps.code:
errors.txt format:

Error: NameError: name total is not defined
Date: [date]
What I was trying to do: add up values in a loop
Cause: I used the variable total before assigning it a starting value
Fix: add total = 0 before the loop
Lesson: always initialise variables before using them
steps.warning: If you ask Replit AI to fix your code and it works but you don't understand why, that is not debugging — that is borrowing a solution. You will encounter the same error pattern again and be equally stuck. The goal is to understand each error well enough that you could explain it to someone else.

walkthroughs.title: Setting up a coding classroom in Replit Teams
walkthroughs.description: Replit Teams for Education transforms Replit from a solo coding tool into a shared classroom environment. You can create projects for students, see their code in real time, leave comments, and track progress — all without anything installed on student devices.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: The biggest advantage of Replit for classroom coding is not the AI — it is that every student is in the same environment, you can see their work without collecting files, and nothing needs to be installed or maintained.

steps.title: Apply for Replit Teams for Education
steps.content: Go to replit.com/teams-for-education. Apply with your school email address. Verification is typically fast. Once approved, you get a free Teams workspace with access to project creation, student progress tracking, code annotations, and multiplayer coding.
steps.tip: Set up your Teams workspace and run through the student experience yourself before your first lesson. Create a test student account and join your own team to see exactly what your students will see.

steps.title: Create a project with clear instructions
steps.content: In Teams, click New Project. Write instructions as if you will not be in the room to answer questions. Include: the goal, what the output should look like, any constraints, and how students will know when they have finished.
steps.code:
Good project instructions template:

Goal: Write a Python program that asks the user for their name and age, then prints a message telling them how old they will be in 10 years.

Your output should look exactly like this:
What is your name? Priya
How old are you? 14
Hi Priya! In 10 years, you'll be 24 years old.

Constraints:
- Use input() to get the name and age from the user
- The age must be converted to an integer using int()

You're done when: running your program produces the exact output format shown above.
steps.tip: Include a sample of what the expected output looks like. This single addition eliminates most questions about whether their solution is correct. Students can run their code, compare it to the expected output, and self-assess before asking for help.

steps.title: Monitor student code in real time
steps.content: In the Teams dashboard, click any student name to open their code. You can see it update in real time as they type. You can leave annotations (comments) directly on specific lines — these appear as side notes the student can read.
steps.code:
Effective annotation patterns:

When stuck: highlight the error line and write: 'This line is trying to add a number to a string. Look up str() conversion in Python.'

When approaching it wrong: 'This will work, but think about what happens if the user types 0. Is that the right behaviour?'

When it is good: 'This works correctly. Challenge: can you make it handle a case where the user types a word instead of a number?'
steps.warning: Don't fix students' code for them — annotate questions that point them toward the fix. A student who fixes their own code with a hint learns more than one whose code was corrected for them.

steps.title: Run the first lesson: the three-program structure
steps.content: For a first coding lesson in Replit, a three-program arc works well. It gives every student a success experience, builds confidence, and introduces the core concepts without overloading.
steps.code:
Three-program first lesson structure:

Program 1 (10 min): Give students a complete, working program. They run it, read it, and change one thing — then run it again. Goal: complete the write-run-see loop with confidence.

Program 2 (15 min): Give students a program with two intentional errors. They find and fix both without being told what is wrong. Goal: read error messages and problem-solve.

Program 3 (20 min): Give students a blank Repl with instructions for a simple program they write themselves. Replit AI is allowed. Goal: experience building something from scratch.
steps.tip: The progression matters: guided then guided error-fixing then open creation. Jumping to open creation in the first lesson produces anxiety and disengagement. The first lesson should leave every student feeling capable, not overwhelmed.

walkthroughs.title: Using the Code Interpreter for data tasks
walkthroughs.description: Code Interpreter (now called Advanced Data Analysis) lets ChatGPT run actual Python code on files you upload — not just talk about data, but compute with it. Upload a spreadsheet and it will analyse, visualise, and summarise it. For educators managing student data, or students working with datasets for projects, this is one of the most practically powerful features in any AI tool.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Code Interpreter turns ChatGPT into a working data analyst. It makes mistakes — especially on assumptions about your data — but it shows you its code, which means you can catch and correct errors in a way you cannot with a black-box tool.

steps.title: Enable Advanced Data Analysis and upload a file
steps.content: In ChatGPT (GPT-4o), click the paperclip icon to attach a file. You can upload CSV, Excel, PDF, image files, and more. When Code Interpreter is active, ChatGPT runs Python on your file rather than just reading it.
steps.code:
File types that work well:
- CSV files: student grades, survey data, attendance records
- Excel (.xlsx): any spreadsheet data
- PDF: it will extract the text and attempt to structure it

File types with limitations:
- Very large Excel files may time out
- Complex multi-sheet workbooks may confuse it — export one sheet at a time
- Scanned PDFs without text layer may not extract well
steps.tip: Before uploading real student data, check your school's data privacy policy. Student grade data, names, and identifiers are personal data. If in doubt: anonymise the data first — replace names with Student A, B, C — or use a sample dataset for exploration.

steps.title: Start with a data description request
steps.content: Always start by asking ChatGPT to describe what it sees in your data before asking it to do analysis. This surfaces any misunderstandings about structure, column names, or data types before they cause silent errors.
steps.code:
Opening prompt:
'Describe the structure of this dataset. How many rows and columns? What does each column appear to contain? Are there any missing values or obvious data quality issues?'

Why this matters:
If ChatGPT misidentifies a column, its subsequent analysis will be silently wrong. The description step forces it to state its assumptions — which you can then correct before it proceeds.
steps.tip: After the description, if anything is wrong — wrong column interpretation, missing data it didn't mention — correct it explicitly before proceeding.

steps.title: Ask for analysis and chart generation
steps.content: Once the data structure is confirmed, ask for the analysis you need. Code Interpreter can generate professional charts, calculate statistics, and produce formatted summaries from plain language instructions.
steps.code:
Useful analysis requests:

For grade data:
'Calculate the class average, highest score, lowest score, and standard deviation for each test. Present as a table.'

'Create a bar chart showing the distribution of grades in five bands: 0-40, 40-55, 55-70, 70-85, 85-100.'

'Identify students who scored below 40% in more than two tests and list their names and scores.'

For attendance data:
'Calculate each student attendance percentage. Highlight anyone below 75%. Create a horizontal bar chart sorted from lowest to highest.'
steps.tip: Ask for charts with specific axis labels, titles, and colour choices. Generic chart requests produce generic charts — specifying the exact labels and format you need produces something you can use directly in a report or presentation.

steps.title: Read the code it ran — don't just read the output
steps.content: Code Interpreter shows you the Python code it ran. Reading it — even if you do not understand all of it — lets you spot when it made a wrong assumption.
steps.code:
Things to check in the code:

1. Which columns did it use? (Check the column names match yours)
2. How did it handle missing values? (Did it drop rows? Fill with zero? This changes your results.)
3. What formula did it use for any calculation?

If you see something wrong:
Tell it: the column it used is actually the student number — the scores are in columns E through J. Redo the analysis using the correct columns.
steps.warning: Code Interpreter can produce charts and statistics that look authoritative but are based on incorrect assumptions about your data. Always verify the output against a manual check on a small sample of your data before presenting it or acting on it.

walkthroughs.title: Using Claude's extended thinking for hard problems
walkthroughs.description: Claude's extended thinking mode makes its reasoning process visible. Rather than jumping to a response, it works through the problem step by step — and shows you that working. For genuinely complex problems where you need to trust the reasoning, not just the conclusion, this is the mode to use.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Extended thinking is useful when the problem has multiple interdependent variables, requires you to see the reasoning (not just the answer), or is the type of problem where a confident wrong answer is worse than a slower correct one.

steps.title: What extended thinking actually does
steps.content: In standard mode, Claude generates a response directly. In extended thinking, it generates a scratchpad of internal reasoning first — working through the problem, considering alternatives, catching its own errors — before producing the final response. You see both the thinking and the conclusion.
steps.tip: Extended thinking is not available in all Claude interfaces. In Claude.ai, it appears as an option for complex queries — look for the thinking toggle or Claude may activate it automatically for problems it assesses as needing deeper reasoning.

steps.title: Problems worth using extended thinking for
steps.content: Extended thinking adds time. Use it selectively — for problems where seeing the reasoning matters or where complexity genuinely benefits from systematic working-through.
steps.code:
Good uses:

Multi-variable decisions:
'I need to decide whether to change our school assessment structure from continuous assessment to end-of-term exams. Factors: student stress levels, teaching flexibility, parental expectations, board requirements, teacher workload. Work through the trade-offs systematically.'

Logical or scheduling problems:
'Solve this scheduling problem: 6 teachers, 8 subjects, 30 periods per week, with these constraints. What is the optimal allocation?'

Not worth it for:
- Simple factual questions
- Standard document analysis
- Writing and editing tasks

steps.title: Read the thinking — don't skip to the conclusion
steps.content: The most common mistake with extended thinking: reading only the final answer and ignoring the thinking block. The thinking is where errors, assumptions, and uncertainties surface.
steps.code:
What to look for in the thinking block:

- Assumptions made about missing information
- Points where Claude considered and rejected alternatives — are those rejections correct?
- Any moment where Claude expresses uncertainty
- The logic chain: does each step follow from the previous one?

If you find a flawed assumption:
Tell Claude: in your thinking you assumed X — that assumption is wrong, Y is actually the case. Can you redo the analysis with the correct assumption?

steps.title: Use it to check your own reasoning, not just generate new reasoning
steps.content: One underused extended thinking application: giving Claude your reasoning and asking it to find the flaws. This is the Socratic use of the tool.
steps.code:
Prompt pattern:

'Here is my reasoning about [problem]. I have reached this conclusion: [your conclusion]. Use extended thinking to work through my reasoning step by step. Identify: (1) any logical steps that do not follow from the previous ones, (2) any assumptions I have made that I have not stated, (3) any alternative conclusions that my evidence could equally support.'
steps.tip: This use of extended thinking is particularly valuable for essay and argument construction — both for your own writing and for teaching students to evaluate the logical structure of their arguments.

walkthroughs.title: Gemini Deep Research: full investigative reports
walkthroughs.description: Gemini Deep Research conducts a multi-step research process: plans the research, searches dozens of sources, synthesises the findings, and produces a structured long-form report. For educators and students who need a comprehensive overview of a topic quickly, it produces outputs that rival a solid first-draft literature review.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Deep Research produces a better-than-average first draft of a research overview. What it cannot do is exercise academic judgment — it does not distinguish strong evidence from weak, or primary research from commentary.

steps.title: Access Deep Research and understand what it costs
steps.content: Deep Research is available in Gemini Advanced (requires a Google One AI Premium subscription) at gemini.google.com. It is also available in limited form to some Google Workspace Education accounts. The free Gemini tier does not include Deep Research.
steps.tip: If Deep Research is not available to your students, Perplexity Pro Search (free with limited daily uses) produces comparable output for most educational research questions. They are genuine alternatives for this task.

steps.title: Give it a specific, scoped research question
steps.content: Deep Research works best with specific, bounded questions. Broad topic areas produce unfocused reports. Specific questions produce focused, usable ones.
steps.code:
Effective Deep Research prompts:

'What does current research say about the effectiveness of project-based learning in secondary school mathematics, and what are the implementation challenges most commonly reported by teachers?'

'Provide a research overview of the National Education Policy 2020 in India — its goals, implementation progress, and the main critiques from education researchers.'

'What are the main theories of second language acquisition, and what does recent research say about which instructional approaches are most effective for adult learners?'
steps.tip: Review the research plan Deep Research generates before it starts searching. If the plan misses an important angle, tell it before it proceeds.

steps.title: Read the report critically — not as a finished product
steps.content: Deep Research produces a long, structured report with citations. It looks authoritative. Treat it as a well-organised first draft that requires critical review.
steps.code:
Verification checklist for any Deep Research output:

1. Click through to at least 5 of the cited sources — do they actually say what the report claims?
2. Check the recency of sources — is the research from the last 3-5 years on a fast-moving topic?
3. Assess source quality — are the citations from peer-reviewed journals, or from news articles and blogs?
4. Look for what is missing — does the report acknowledge limitations, or does it present a falsely confident synthesis?
5. Check for positions the report did not represent — are there credible dissenting views not included?
steps.warning: Deep Research's citation accuracy is higher than ChatGPT's but not perfect. It sometimes misrepresents the strength or direction of a cited finding. For any claim you plan to use in teaching or share as research evidence, verify it directly from the source.

steps.title: Export and use the report as a scaffold
steps.content: The Deep Research report can be exported to Google Docs. Once in Docs, use Gemini sidebar to ask follow-up questions about specific sections, add your own analysis, or ask it to expand particular points.
steps.tip: For student research assignments: Deep Research is most valuable as a scoping tool. It tells students what the major themes, findings, and debates in a field are — so they can make informed choices about which specific question to pursue and which sources to read. Assign it at the beginning of a research project, not as a replacement for original research.

walkthroughs.title: What makes Khanmigo different from ChatGPT for studying
walkthroughs.description: Most AI tools give you answers. Khanmigo deliberately does not. It was designed with one principle: giving a student the answer to a maths problem or an essay question teaches them nothing. Instead it asks questions, offers hints, and guides you toward working it out yourself. This walkthrough explains why that matters and when to use each tool.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Khanmigo is the right tool when you want to actually learn something. ChatGPT is the right tool when you need an answer quickly. Using ChatGPT to study is like using a calculator before you understand what multiplication is.

steps.title: The core design difference
steps.content: ChatGPT is a completion engine — it generates the most likely continuation of whatever you give it. If you give it a maths problem, it completes it with a solution. If you give it an essay prompt, it completes it with an essay. Khanmigo was built on a different principle: it is a Socratic tutor, not an answer machine. When you ask it a question, it asks one back.
steps.code:
What happens when you ask each tool the same question:

You: 'What is the quadratic formula and how do I use it?'

ChatGPT: [gives you the formula, explains it, provides worked examples]

Khanmigo: 'Great question! Before I give you the formula, can you tell me what a quadratic equation looks like? What makes an equation quadratic rather than linear?'

The difference: ChatGPT transfers information. Khanmigo checks whether you already have the foundation and builds from what you actually know.
steps.tip: If you are in a hurry and just need the answer: use ChatGPT. If you are studying for an exam and want to actually understand the material: use Khanmigo. The tool choice is a decision about your goal, not about which tool is better.

steps.title: When Khanmigo's approach is a genuine advantage
steps.content: The Socratic method is not just philosophy — it is one of the most evidence-backed approaches to learning. Being asked to retrieve and apply knowledge is more effective for retention than being shown the same knowledge passively. Khanmigo's design forces active recall and application rather than passive reading of an explanation.
steps.code:
Situations where Khanmigo's approach beats ChatGPT:

- Exam preparation: working through problems with guided hints builds the retrieval pathways you need in an exam room, where there is no AI
- Understanding not just knowing: if you need to apply a concept in different contexts, understanding it matters more than memorising the answer
- Writing and argumentation: Khanmigo's essay feedback asks you to improve your own argument rather than rewriting it for you
- Maths and science problem sets: guided hints on your specific mistake are more useful than a fully worked solution you read passively
steps.tip: Use Khanmigo for the topics you find hardest — the ones where you are most tempted to just look up the answer. The resistance you feel when it asks you a question instead of giving you the answer is the feeling of learning.

steps.title: Setting up access — free vs paid
steps.content: Khanmigo is built into Khan Academy. Go to khanacademy.org and create a free account. Khanmigo itself requires a paid subscription (currently a monthly or annual fee), but Khan Academy's core content — videos, exercises, and practice problems — is completely free and is where Khanmigo draws its curriculum from. For students in India: Khan Academy content is available in Hindi and several regional languages.
steps.code:
Access options:

Free: All Khan Academy exercises, videos, and practice sets — no Khanmigo
Paid: Khanmigo AI tutor on top of all free content

For educators: Khan Academy for Teachers is free and includes classroom tools, progress tracking, and assignment creation. Khanmigo for teachers includes additional tools like lesson idea generation and student support features.
steps.tip: Even without Khanmigo, Khan Academy's practice exercise system has built-in hints and step-by-step solutions that function as a structured tutor. If you cannot afford Khanmigo, the free exercises plus the hint system give you most of the benefit for maths and science subjects.

steps.title: The one thing Khanmigo will not do — and why that is the point
steps.content: Khanmigo will not write your essay, solve your problem set, or complete your homework for you. If you ask it to, it will decline and offer to help you work through it instead. Some students find this frustrating. That frustration is worth examining — because the discomfort of not getting the answer handed to you is precisely what drives the learning process.
steps.warning: If you find yourself frustrated that Khanmigo will not just give you the answer: that is a signal that you are approaching it as a shortcut tool rather than a learning tool. The two tools are for different goals. There is no judgment in using ChatGPT for tasks where you need an answer — but be honest with yourself about whether the task is learning or task completion.
steps.tip: Ask Khanmigo: 'I am completely stuck and do not know where to start. Can you give me just the first step?' It will usually give you a genuine first foothold — not the full solution, but enough to move forward. This is actually the most useful hint structure for genuine understanding.

walkthroughs.title: Using Khanmigo as a maths tutor: worked examples and hints
walkthroughs.description: Maths is where Khanmigo earns its reputation. Unlike a generalist AI that will just solve a problem, Khanmigo identifies where exactly in the working you went wrong and asks the question that reveals the gap. This walkthrough shows the interaction patterns that make maths tutoring with Khanmigo actually effective.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: The most valuable thing Khanmigo does in maths is not give you the answer — it identifies which specific step you are stuck on and gives you a hint for exactly that step. This is what a good human tutor does, and it is far more effective than a worked solution.

steps.title: Start by showing your working, not just the problem
steps.content: When you bring a maths problem to Khanmigo, do not just paste the question. Show what you have tried so far, even if it is wrong. This gives Khanmigo something specific to work with — it can identify where your reasoning broke down rather than starting from scratch.
steps.code:
Less useful:
'Solve: 3x² + 5x - 2 = 0'

More useful:
'I am trying to solve 3x² + 5x - 2 = 0 using the quadratic formula. I got x = (-5 ± √(25 + 24)) / 6. I think that simplifies to x = (-5 ± 7) / 6, giving me x = 1/3 or x = -2. But my textbook says the answer is different. Where did I go wrong?'

Khanmigo can now identify that your working is actually correct (the textbook may have a typo, or you may be reading the wrong answer) rather than assuming you made an error.
steps.tip: Even if your working is completely wrong, showing it is more useful than hiding it. The specific nature of your error tells Khanmigo exactly which concept needs reinforcement.

steps.title: Use the hint ladder — one hint at a time
steps.content: When Khanmigo offers to give you a hint, ask for the smallest possible hint first. Do not ask for the full explanation. Work with each hint before asking for the next. This is the hint ladder — and climbing it slowly is far more effective for learning than jumping to the bottom rung.
steps.code:
Hint ladder in practice:

You: 'I am stuck on how to factor x² - 5x + 6. Can you give me a small hint?'

Khanmigo: 'Think about two numbers that multiply to give 6 and add to give -5. What pairs of numbers multiply to 6?'

You: '1 and 6, or 2 and 3.'

Khanmigo: 'Good. Now which of those pairs could add to give -5 if we make one or both of them negative?'

You: '-2 and -3 — they multiply to 6 and add to -5.'

Khanmigo: 'Exactly. So how does that help you write the factored form?'

This conversation produces understanding. Reading a worked solution does not.
steps.tip: If you get the answer after a hint, say it back to Khanmigo in your own words: 'So the factored form is (x-2)(x-3) because those two brackets expand back to give us the original equation, right?' Making yourself articulate the logic cements it.

steps.title: Ask for a similar problem to test yourself
steps.content: After working through a problem with Khanmigo's help, ask it to give you a similar problem at the same difficulty level. Solve it independently. This is the test of whether you understood the concept or just followed the steps.
steps.code:
After solving a problem:
'Now give me a similar factoring problem at the same difficulty. I will try it on my own first and come back if I get stuck.'

If you solve it without hints: the concept is consolidated.
If you need hints again: the concept is not yet secure — ask Khanmigo to identify which specific part is still unclear.
If you get it wrong in a different way: a new gap has been identified — ask Khanmigo about the new error specifically.
steps.tip: Ask for progressively harder variations: 'Now give me one that is slightly harder — maybe with a coefficient in front of x².' Stretching the difficulty incrementally builds the kind of flexible understanding that performs well in exams, not just in practice.

steps.title: Use Khanmigo alongside Khan Academy exercises — not instead of them
steps.content: Khanmigo is most powerful when used in combination with Khan Academy's structured exercise sets. Work through the exercises — they give you immediate feedback on right and wrong answers. When you get something wrong and the hint system does not fully explain why, bring the specific problem to Khanmigo for a deeper explanation.
steps.code:
Optimal workflow:

1. Do a Khan Academy exercise set on the topic
2. When you get a problem wrong: read the hint system's explanation first
3. If still unclear: bring the problem to Khanmigo with your specific confusion: 'I got this problem wrong. The hint said to do X. I do not understand why X works here.'
4. Work through the Khanmigo explanation using the hint ladder
5. Go back to the exercise set and try more problems of the same type
6. Repeat until you complete the exercise set without needing hints
steps.warning: Do not skip to Khanmigo before trying the problem yourself and reading the Khan Academy hints first. The struggle of attempting the problem before receiving help is where most of the learning happens. Khanmigo is for when you are genuinely stuck — not for before you have tried.

walkthroughs.title: Debate Partner and Essay Feedback modes
walkthroughs.description: Khanmigo has two modes that most students do not know about: Debate Partner, where it argues the opposite position to whatever you take, and Essay Feedback, where it evaluates your writing and asks you questions to improve it. Both are significantly better for developing thinking skills than the ChatGPT equivalent.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Khanmigo's essay feedback does not rewrite your essay — it asks you questions that help you rewrite it yourself. This is slower and harder than asking ChatGPT. It is also the only version that actually improves your writing.

steps.title: Debate Partner: how to use it and what it is for
steps.content: Khanmigo's Debate Partner mode argues the opposite position to whatever stance you take — and it does not let up. It raises counterarguments, challenges your evidence, and pushes back on weak reasoning. This is one of the most underused study tools available to students preparing for argumentative essays or discussions.
steps.code:
How to start a debate:

Tell Khanmigo the topic and your position:
'I want to practice debating. My position is: social media does more harm than good for teenagers. Take the opposing side and argue against me. Push back hard on my weakest points.'

What to do during the debate:
- State your argument
- When Khanmigo pushes back: do not just repeat your argument louder. Find new evidence or refine your reasoning.
- When you cannot counter a point: note it. That is a genuine weakness in your argument that needs addressing.
- At the end, ask Khanmigo: 'What were the three strongest points I made, and the three weakest?'
steps.tip: Before writing any argumentative essay, run a 10-minute Debate Partner session on your thesis. The counterarguments Khanmigo raises are likely the same ones your teacher or examiner will have. Address them in your essay before they can be raised.

steps.title: Essay Feedback: the right way to use it
steps.content: Paste your essay into Khanmigo and ask for feedback. Unlike ChatGPT, which will rewrite sections or offer you a 'better' version, Khanmigo will ask you questions that help you identify what is weak and how to fix it yourself.
steps.code:
Prompt to use:
'Here is my essay: [paste essay]. Please give me feedback. Do not rewrite any part of it. Ask me questions that help me identify what needs to be improved and how I might improve it.'

What Khanmigo typically asks:
- 'Your introduction states your thesis, but what specific evidence are you planning to use to support it? Is that clear to the reader from this opening?'
- 'In paragraph 3, you make a strong claim. What is the source of that claim? Would a reader find it convincing without a citation?'
- 'Your conclusion summarises the essay — but does it advance the argument beyond what you said in the introduction? What new insight does it leave the reader with?'
steps.tip: Answer Khanmigo's questions in the chat first — write out your answers before going back to edit your essay. The act of articulating the answer in the chat clarifies what you need to change. Then go back to the essay with a clear idea of what to fix.

steps.title: Using feedback to build a revision checklist
steps.content: After a full essay feedback session with Khanmigo, ask it to summarise the key issues it identified as a checklist. Use this checklist every time you write — the patterns in what Khanmigo flags repeatedly are the specific weaknesses in your writing that need the most work.
steps.code:
After the feedback session:
'Based on our conversation about this essay, can you give me a personalised revision checklist — the specific things I should check before submitting any essay, based on the issues you found in this one?'

Example output:
[ ] Does my introduction state a specific, arguable thesis (not just a topic)?
[ ] Does every paragraph have one clear main claim?
[ ] Does every claim have specific supporting evidence, not just a general statement?
[ ] Have I addressed the strongest counterargument directly?
[ ] Does my conclusion add something beyond summarising the body paragraphs?
[ ] Have I removed any sentences that do not directly support my main argument?
steps.warning: Do not use this checklist as a box-ticking exercise. For each item, read the relevant part of your essay and genuinely ask whether it meets the criterion. A checklist completed without attention is worthless — the thinking is the point, not the ticks.

walkthroughs.title: Your first AI voiceover in under 5 minutes
walkthroughs.description: ElevenLabs turns written text into speech that sounds like a real person recorded it in a studio. The quality difference between ElevenLabs and older text-to-speech tools is significant enough that the output is usable in professional contexts — educational videos, accessibility materials, podcasts, and presentations. This walkthrough gets you to your first audio file in minutes.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: ElevenLabs' output quality makes it useful for real educational content — not just a novelty. The free tier is enough to evaluate whether it fits your workflow before committing to anything.

steps.title: Create your account and understand the free tier
steps.content: Go to elevenlabs.io and create a free account. The free tier gives you a limited number of characters per month (enough for short projects and evaluation). No credit card required. Once inside, you will see the Text to Speech interface — this is where you will spend most of your time.
steps.tip: The free tier resets monthly. If you are planning a specific project, check how many characters it will require before starting. A typical 5-minute educational voiceover script is approximately 3,500 to 4,000 characters — well within the free monthly allowance for a single project.

steps.title: Write or paste your script — and format it for speech
steps.content: In the Text to Speech panel, paste the text you want to convert. Written text and spoken text are not the same thing. Before generating, read your script out loud. If it sounds unnatural when you say it, it will sound unnatural when the AI says it.
steps.code:
Text that reads well but sounds wrong spoken:
'The mitochondria, as previously established, is responsible for adenosine triphosphate synthesis.'

Text written for the ear:
'We have already seen that the mitochondria has one main job: making energy. It does this by producing a molecule called ATP — adenosine triphosphate — which the cell uses as fuel.'

Formatting tips:
- Use commas and full stops where you want pauses — the AI respects punctuation
- Spell out acronyms on first use: 'DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid)'
- Write numbers as words if you want them spoken naturally: 'twenty-three' not '23'
- Use ellipses (...) for a longer pause where needed
steps.tip: If the AI mispronounces a specific word — a technical term, a name, a local place name — ElevenLabs has a pronunciation dictionary where you can add custom pronunciations using phonetic spelling.

steps.title: Choose a voice and adjust settings
steps.content: Click the voice selector. ElevenLabs has a library of pre-made voices — browse by gender, accent, and use case. For educational content, look for voices tagged 'narration' or 'educational'. Try three or four voices on a short sample of your text before committing — voices sound different at different speeds and with different content.
steps.code:
Settings to adjust:

Stability: higher = more consistent, lower = more expressive variation. For narration, 60-75% stability works well. For something more dramatic or conversational, try 40-55%.

Similarity Enhancement: how closely the output matches the voice model. Keep this at 75% or above unless you want more variation.

Style Exaggeration (where available): adds emphasis and personality. Use sparingly for educational content — too high makes the voice sound theatrical.

Speaker Boost: improves clarity for some voices. Turn on if the voice sounds slightly muffled.
steps.tip: Generate a 10-15 second sample before generating the full script. Adjust settings based on the sample. Regenerating the full script after finding the right settings is much faster than adjusting after the fact.

steps.title: Download and use your audio
steps.content: Click Generate. When complete, click Download to save as an MP3. The file is ready to use in: video editors (DaVinci Resolve free, CapCut, iMovie), presentation tools (Canva, PowerPoint with audio), podcast platforms, or as a standalone audio file shared with students.
steps.code:
Common educational uses:

Video narration: import the MP3 into a video editor, add your slides or visuals as a separate track

Audio worksheet: convert written explanations into an audio version for students who benefit from hearing content

Podcast-style lesson summary: script a 3-5 minute summary of a lesson, generate it with ElevenLabs, share as audio

Accessibility: create audio versions of all printed classroom materials for students with reading difficulties or visual impairments
steps.warning: Always label ElevenLabs-generated audio as AI-generated when sharing it with students or parents. This is an ethical requirement, not just a courtesy — people have a right to know whether they are hearing a real person or a synthetic voice.

walkthroughs.title: Creating accessible audio versions of classroom materials
walkthroughs.description: Printed materials are inaccessible to students with dyslexia, visual impairments, low literacy, or language barriers. ElevenLabs makes it practical for a single teacher to produce audio versions of every handout, worksheet, and reading — in a realistic voice, in minutes, at no cost on the free tier. This walkthrough builds that workflow.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Accessibility is not an extra — it is part of good teaching. ElevenLabs removes the time cost that previously made audio materials impractical for individual teachers to produce.

steps.title: Identify which materials benefit most from audio versions
steps.content: Not every piece of classroom material needs an audio version — prioritise the ones where reading difficulty creates the biggest barrier to learning.
steps.code:
High priority for audio versions:
- Core explanatory texts: the materials that explain key concepts students need to understand
- Exam preparation materials: revision guides, question papers with instructions
- Homework instructions: students who misread instructions lose marks for content they understand
- Story or source texts used in comprehension exercises
- Any material that students need to engage with independently

Lower priority:
- Exercises and worksheets where the student is producing output (not just reading)
- Reference tables and data sheets (these are better as visual materials)
- Anything where scanning and searching the text is the main activity
steps.tip: Ask students directly which materials they find hardest to access. The answer is often more specific than teachers expect — one particular type of question wording, one specific subject's reading load, one dense textbook chapter.

steps.title: Adapt the text for spoken delivery before generating
steps.content: Textbook prose, exam question language, and formal handout text are all written for the eye. Before generating audio, rewrite the key passages slightly for the ear — this takes 5 to 10 minutes and significantly improves comprehension for audio listeners.
steps.code:
Typical adaptations:

Original: 'Refer to the diagram on page 3, Figure 2.1, and identify the three key components labelled A, B, and C.'
Adapted: 'In your handout, look at the diagram on page 3 — it is labelled Figure 2.1. The diagram has three components labelled A, B, and C. We will go through each one.'

Original: 'N.B. Students must complete sections 1-3 before attempting section 4.'
Adapted: 'Important note: complete sections 1, 2, and 3 before you move on to section 4.'

Original: 'See overleaf.'
Adapted: 'Turn over the page.'
steps.tip: Create a find-and-replace list for the most common written-only phrases in your materials: 'see above', 'as follows', 'N.B.', 'i.e.', 'e.g.', 'ibid.' — replace them with their spoken equivalents before running anything through ElevenLabs.

steps.title: Build a consistent voice and format for your class
steps.content: Choose one voice for all your class's audio materials and use it consistently. Students who rely on audio materials build familiarity with a specific voice — switching voices across different materials creates an unnecessary cognitive adjustment.
steps.code:
Setting up a consistent audio format:

1. Choose one voice from the ElevenLabs library and save it as your default
2. Save your preferred stability and similarity settings
3. Add a standard spoken introduction to every audio file: 'This is the audio version of [material name] for [class]. Duration: approximately [X] minutes.'
4. Save all audio files with a consistent naming format: 'Class8-Science-Photosynthesis-Audio.mp3'
5. Upload to a consistent location: a shared Google Drive folder, Google Classroom, or school platform
steps.warning: Test every audio file by listening to the first 30 seconds before distributing. ElevenLabs occasionally mispronounces subject-specific vocabulary, proper nouns, or numbers formatted in unusual ways. Catching one mispronunciation before distribution saves significant confusion later.

steps.title: Multilingual audio: reaching students whose first language is not English
steps.content: ElevenLabs supports audio generation in multiple languages including Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, and other Indian languages, as well as major world languages. For classes with students whose first language is not the language of instruction, a translated audio version of core materials can be transformative.
steps.code:
Workflow for multilingual audio:

1. Take your core explanation text
2. Use Claude or ChatGPT to translate it into the target language — specify: 'Translate this for spoken audio, not written text. Use natural spoken [language] that a student would hear from a teacher.'
3. Review the translation with a speaker of that language if possible
4. Paste into ElevenLabs and select a voice for that language
5. Generate and download

Note: always have a fluent speaker review translations of technical content before sharing with students. AI translation of subject-specific vocabulary is not always accurate in all languages.
steps.tip: Even a translated audio introduction to a lesson — a 2-minute spoken overview of what the lesson is about and what students will learn — can significantly improve comprehension for students learning through a second language.

walkthroughs.title: Voice cloning: what it is, how it works, and the ethics
walkthroughs.description: ElevenLabs can clone a voice from a sample recording — producing speech that sounds like a specific real person. This capability is genuinely useful and genuinely dangerous, sometimes simultaneously. This walkthrough explains the technology, the legitimate uses, and the ethical lines that must not be crossed.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Voice cloning is one of the most ethically consequential AI capabilities available to the general public. The only voices you may clone are your own, or voices for which you have explicit, informed, written consent from the person whose voice it is.

steps.title: What voice cloning actually does
steps.content: ElevenLabs' voice cloning takes a recording of a person speaking — as little as one minute of audio — and creates a voice model that can generate new speech in that person's voice, saying anything you type. The output quality is high enough to be convincing to most listeners, especially for short clips.
steps.tip: Instant Voice Cloning (free tier) requires a short sample and produces a reasonable approximation. Professional Voice Cloning (paid) requires more audio and produces a significantly more accurate model. For legitimate educational uses — cloning your own voice for accessibility — Instant Voice Cloning is usually sufficient.

steps.title: Legitimate uses of voice cloning in education
steps.content: There are genuine educational use cases for voice cloning that do not raise ethical concerns — specifically when you are cloning your own voice with your own consent.
steps.code:
Legitimate educational uses:

Teacher's own voice for audio materials:
Record yourself speaking for 5-10 minutes. Clone your voice. Now generate audio versions of all your handouts in your own voice — students hear their actual teacher, not a generic AI voice. Significantly better for trust and familiarity.

Students creating accessible versions of their own presentations:
A student clones their own voice and uses it to generate an audio version of a written report — useful for students who struggle with public speaking but have strong written work.

Language learning: clone your voice and generate content in a target language — useful for self-study of pronunciation and speech patterns.
steps.warning: You may only clone your own voice without additional consent requirements. Cloning anyone else's voice — a student, a colleague, a public figure, a family member — without their explicit informed written consent is unethical and in many jurisdictions illegal, regardless of your intended use.

steps.title: What voice cloning must never be used for
steps.content: ElevenLabs has terms of service prohibiting misuse, but the ethical obligations go beyond what the platform enforces. Understanding these limits is part of being a responsible AI user and teacher.
steps.code:
Never use voice cloning for:

- Generating audio that makes a real person appear to say something they did not say
- Cloning a student's voice for any purpose without their and their parent's explicit consent
- Creating content that could damage a person's reputation
- Bypassing academic integrity requirements (submitting AI-voiced audio as your own recorded speech)
- Generating fake testimonials, fake interviews, or fake statements attributed to real people
- Any content designed to deceive a listener about who is speaking

Note: 'I did not mean any harm' is not a defence. The harm from fake audio of a real person is caused by the audio existing and being shared, regardless of intent.
steps.tip: Teach this to students explicitly and early. Voice cloning tools are accessible to anyone with a phone. Students need to understand the ethical and legal framework around synthetic media before they encounter it as a creative option — not after.

steps.title: Teaching students to recognise AI-generated audio
steps.content: Just as with AI video, the most important media literacy skill around audio is being able to question whether what you are hearing is real. AI audio is already being used in scams, political manipulation, and fraud. Students who understand how it works are harder to deceive.
steps.code:
Signs of AI-generated audio (current generation):
- Unusually consistent pacing — no natural breath or rhythm variation in longer sections
- Mispronunciation of unusual proper nouns, local names, or subject-specific terms
- No background noise, breath sounds, or room acoustics at all (unnaturally clean)
- Emotional tone that does not vary naturally with the content
- Slight robotic quality at the end of sentences

Classroom activity: play students three short audio clips — one recorded naturally, one generated by ElevenLabs, one from an older text-to-speech system. Ask them to identify which is which and what signals they used.
steps.warning: As AI audio quality improves, the signals above become less reliable. The habit to build is not specific detection skills but a general reflex: for any audio making a consequential claim — about a real person, about a real event — ask 'how do I know this is genuine?' before sharing or acting on it.

walkthroughs.title: Your first recording: transcribing a lecture or meeting
walkthroughs.description: Otter.ai turns spoken audio into searchable, summarised text in real time. For students who struggle to take notes while listening, or who want to review exactly what was said in a lecture, it is one of the most practically useful tools on this list. This walkthrough gets you recording and transcribing in minutes.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Otter is most valuable when listening and writing at the same time is genuinely difficult — for students with dyslexia, ADHD, or English as a second language, or in fast-paced lectures where note-taking competes with comprehension.

steps.title: Set up Otter.ai and understand the free tier
steps.content: Go to otter.ai and create a free account (also available as a mobile app for Android and iOS). The free tier gives you a set number of transcription minutes per month — enough for regular use for most students. The app is more useful than the website for recording lectures, because your phone is already in your pocket.
steps.tip: On the mobile app, enable Otter's notification permissions and microphone access during setup. Both are required for real-time transcription to work correctly. If you set it up but the transcription is not running, check that microphone permissions were granted.

steps.title: Start a recording in a lecture or meeting
steps.content: Open the Otter app and tap the record button. Otter begins transcribing immediately. Place your phone on the desk in front of you with the microphone facing the speaker — do not keep it in your pocket. During the recording, you can tap on words in the transcript to add notes or highlights at specific moments.
steps.code:
During a lecture — what to do:

- Set your phone on the desk, screen up, microphone toward the speaker
- Let Otter run in the background — you do not need to watch it
- Focus on listening and understanding, not on writing
- If a key point is made: tap the screen and add a quick note or star that moment
- When the lecture ends: tap Stop

What Otter does automatically:
- Transcribes every word
- Identifies different speakers where possible
- Generates a summary with key points
- Makes the transcript searchable
steps.tip: Otter works best when the speaker is within 3 to 4 metres of your phone and the room is not too noisy. In a large lecture hall, sit closer to the front than you normally would — transcription accuracy drops significantly with distance and ambient noise.

steps.title: Review, search, and export your notes
steps.content: After recording, open the transcript. You can read the full text, search for specific words or phrases, play back the audio from any point in the transcript by clicking on the word, and export the notes in several formats.
steps.code:
Most useful review actions:

Search: type any word or phrase to jump to every moment it was mentioned — useful for finding when a key term was explained

Playback from transcript: click any word to hear the audio from that exact moment — useful when the transcript is unclear or when you want to hear the exact phrasing

Highlighting: highlight key passages in the transcript the same way you would highlight a printed document

Export options: plain text (for pasting into notes), PDF (for saving), or SRT subtitle file (for adding captions to a video)
steps.tip: Export your Otter notes to a document and use Claude or ChatGPT to generate structured study notes from the transcript. Paste the transcript and ask: 'Convert this lecture transcript into structured study notes with headings, key terms defined, and three practice questions at the end.'

steps.title: Use AI summary — and verify it
steps.content: Otter generates an AI summary of each recording — a bulleted list of the main points. This is useful as a starting point for review but should not replace reading the full transcript for important content.
steps.code:
How to use the summary well:

1. Read the summary first to get the overall shape of the content
2. Identify any point in the summary that is unclear or that you do not remember
3. Search the full transcript for that point and read the fuller context
4. For any key definition or explanation: play back the audio from that moment to hear it in the speaker's exact words

Why the summary is not enough:
- AI summaries omit nuance and emphasis
- They sometimes summarise incorrect transcription (mishearing changes meaning)
- They cannot replace your judgment about what matters for your specific exam or assignment
steps.warning: Otter's transcription accuracy depends heavily on audio quality, speaker accent, and background noise. Always review the transcript for obvious errors — especially for subject-specific vocabulary, numbers, names, and technical terms — before using it as a study source.

walkthroughs.title: Privacy, consent, and responsible use of recording tools
walkthroughs.description: Recording a conversation without consent is illegal in many jurisdictions and is a serious breach of trust in any context. This walkthrough covers what you must do before recording any person with Otter or any other recording tool — and why the ethical obligations exist independently of the law.
walkthroughs.keyTakeaway: Recording someone without their knowledge or consent is wrong. The fact that the technology makes it easy does not change the ethical or legal obligation. Ask before you record — every time.

steps.title: The consent requirement — what it is and why it exists
steps.content: Recording a conversation is not a neutral act. The people being recorded have not agreed to have their words transcribed, stored, processed by an AI, or shared with anyone else. In many countries, recording without consent is a criminal offence. In all contexts, it is a violation of the trust of the people being recorded.
steps.code:
Consent requirements vary by context:

Lectures and classes:
Many institutions allow students to record for personal accessibility purposes. Check your institution's policy. If a lecturer says 'please do not record this session', you must stop recording immediately — regardless of your reason for recording.

Meetings with colleagues or teachers:
Always ask explicitly before recording. 'Is it alright if I record this meeting for my own notes? I will not share the recording.' A verbal yes is the minimum — for formal meetings, written consent is better.

Group study sessions:
All participants must consent. Asking one person is not enough if five people are present.

Public lectures or events explicitly marked as recordable:
Consent is typically given by the event organisers for the audience. Check signage or event information.
steps.tip: Build the habit of asking before every recording, even when you are confident the answer will be yes. The habit protects you and normalises consent as part of recording culture — which benefits everyone.

steps.title: What happens to your recordings — and who can see them
steps.content: Otter stores your recordings and transcripts on its servers. This means the content of conversations you record — including other people's words — is being processed and stored by a third-party company. This has implications for what you should and should not record.
steps.code:
Do not record with Otter:
- Confidential conversations (medical, legal, HR, counselling)
- Conversations where participants have not consented to cloud storage of their words
- Any conversation where the content is sensitive enough that a data breach would cause harm
- Conversations about other people who are not present and have not consented

For highly sensitive recordings where you need transcription:
- Consider local transcription tools that do not upload to the cloud
- Or take manual notes and transcribe only the non-sensitive portions
steps.warning: Student conversations, student data, and anything said in a safeguarding context must never be recorded with a cloud transcription tool without explicit institutional permission. Check your school's data protection policy before using Otter in any professional context.

steps.title: Teaching students about recording consent
steps.content: Students carry recording devices in their pockets at all times. Many have never been explicitly taught that recording without consent is wrong — they assume that because they could do it, it must be acceptable. This is a media literacy lesson worth teaching explicitly.
steps.code:
Discussion questions for students:

'If you recorded a conversation between two classmates arguing without telling them, and shared the recording with others — what harm could that cause?'

'If a teacher said something in class that you thought was unfair, and you recorded it to show your parents — is that different? Why or why not?'

'If you used Otter to transcribe a private conversation and then shared the transcript — is that different from sharing a recording? Why?'

'What would you want someone to ask you before recording a conversation you were part of?'
steps.tip: Ground the discussion in concrete scenarios before moving to principles. Students who understand the specific harms that recording without consent can cause — embarrassment, reputation damage, breach of trust, legal consequences — are much more likely to internalise the norm than students who are just told it is against the rules.

walkthroughs.title: Generate a full flashcard set from your notes or a topic
walkthroughs.description: Quizlet AI can turn a block of notes, a textbook passage, or a topic name into a complete flashcard set in seconds.
